#8373. PCT Week 20: Home Stretch

📍 Mile 2,594.3 | 🥾 5.88 km | ⛰️ +339m / -55m

Rain had gently drizzled all night, and was still going when I woke up. I was eager to make it to town ASAP, in case it worsened, so packed quickly and was on the way as soon as I could. It was only five miles to Rainy Pass – apparently, a very apt name – and they disappeared quickly.

Unfortunately, getting a hitch didn’t come nearly as quickly. Cars zoomed past us, and we had to laugh at the number of times the drivers pointedly looked at the mountains on the opposite side of the road, as if they didn’t see us. I began waving to every car that passed and finally we had some luck: a van passed us, but turned around and came back to give us a lift. The driver turned out to have once attempted to hike the PCT, but had broken his foot on day three. Rough go. He was heading to Winthrop, which was further away than Mazama but had a bigger supermarket, so that suited us perfectly. And, by pure happenstance, Catch, Sabretooth and Shakedown happened to be trying to hitch there right as we were driving past; the driver stopped and let them pile into the back with me.

This resupply was a little different than usual. It was our final one of the PCT! After eating instant potatoes and tuna for literally every trail dinner since Julian in the desert, I’d finally reached saturation point and had to switch to ramen. We all bought a few of our favourite snacks and treats, and then had a fun little debate over near the alcohol about what we’d need for the terminus. In the end, we all got some form of bubbly, and a few of us grabbed some extras as well. Then we went in search of a town meal.

After a delicious burger at Three Fingered Jack’s Saloon, we were just preparing to try our luck hitching to Mazama when the heavens suddenly opened and rain bucketed down. It was torrential. Immediately we decided to go and grab a coffee at the bakery and wait it out. Of course, as soon as we had our coffees in hand, the rain stopped. When we did make it around to hitching, we didn’t have to wait long and got a lift with one of the first cars that drove by.

The hostel was practically crawling with hikers who, like us, were waiting out the bad weather but planning to start their terminus push tomorrow. In some ways it was overwhelming. I didn’t want to spend energy making new friends when we almost certainly were never going to see them again – a lot of people were heading up to Harts Pass, whereas we were going back to Rainy. But on the other hand it was nice to see a few familiar faces pass through. Apparently Sass and I had just missed Pieces, who’d left that morning. But Alice was still there, and then some hikers we’d been leapfrogging since the desert swung by to say hi after bagging the terminus. More and more hikers trickled in throughout the afternoon as we lazed on the outdoor couches beneath the dry marquee, enjoying the gas-powered fire at our feet and cooing at a puppy belonging to one of the trail angels helping out at the hostel.

📍 Mile 2,619.5 | 🥾 42.15 km | ⛰️ +1,777m / -1,235m

We’d signed up for a shuttle to Rainy Pass, but there were so many hikers heading back to trail this morning that we missed out on the first run. So we decided to try our luck hitching, in case that would get us there faster than the second run. We left early, hoping to beat other hikers who had the same idea, but when we reached the road we discovered we weren’t that early after all. There was no point in so many of us trying to hitch at once, so Sabretooth and I volunteered to do a coffee run while we waited our turn.

Coffees in hand, we were just leaving the courtyard of the Mazama bakery, when I tripped on a crack in the concrete. Before I knew it I was sprawled on the ground, embarrassed by the sympathetic “ooh”s from onlookers who’d seen me tumble. It was quite a fall. I had an open wound the size of an Aussie 5 cent piece on my palm, and I’d scratched up my legs pretty badly, too. It was a little ironic that I’d managed to sustain my worst PCT injury in town rather than on trail. I had, at least, managed to save my coffee – the cup was a little bent, but the contents were fine. But I’d been carrying Catch’s coffee, too, and it hadn’t survived. As I cleaned myself up Sabretooth ordered him another, and then I very carefully picked my way across the concrete and back to the road. By the time we got there the boys had gotten a hitch, but luckily the first car that saw us stopped and delivered us all the way up to Rainy Pass.

It was significantly colder at the pass. Sass and Catch were running laps of the car park to stay warm while they waited for us. We got on trail quickly, climbing higher still and yet naively hoping the day would warm up. Instead, we walked into lightly falling snow. It was magical, coating the ground and the trees in a light dusting of white. Then we arrived at the larches, which are conifers with needles that turn an indescribably gorgeous gold. Unfortunately, Cutthroat Pass was pretty socked in when we arrived, but we were in good spirits when we hit the 2600 milestone – only 50 or so to go! And only a mile or so later, the clouds began to disappear, giving way to a clear azure sky. Snow lay across the mountaintops as if someone had draped a cotton sheet.

We ran into a group of five hikers, overtaking them. They soon caught up with us again and we offered to let them go ahead, but for some reason they decided to tailgate us instead. So we stopped for lunch to put some distance between us. And it turned out to be a good call; a few rays of sunlight warmed us as we gazed around the mountains, taking in the colours of early winter. And when we set off again we soon reentered forest, so we were glad we’d stopped when we had a view.

The walking was nice and easy for several hours, but the final few miles of the day were a climb. It wasn’t a difficult grade, and we were soon above the trees and enjoying the mountain views once again, but I grew tired and was relieved when we made it to the top. Sunset seemed to be kicking off earlier than usual and the colours were unreal. The fading light turned the mountains indigo, which seemed to make the larches glow.

We arrived at camp, pitched quickly, and agreed we’d all be eating dinner from the comfort of our quilts, inside our respective tents. But that didn’t stop us chatting for an hour as we ate.

📍 Mile 2,649 | 🥾 49.9 km | ⛰️ +1,761m / -1,888m

I slept terribly. It was positively freezing last night, and we all woke up to frost on our tents. And to make matters worse, my inflatable sleeping pad was barely lasting for two hours – so I’d had to blow it up constantly throughout the night. I was glad when morning came and I could get moving to stay warm.

I’d been tempted to night hike last night, just because the weather was definitely closing in and I wanted to make it to Canada and back out quickly. But when we’d seen the trail continued along a ridgeline all thoughts of night hiking had disappeared. And this morning I was very pleased with that choice. The trail wrapped around the mountaintops, beckoning me forward into the beautiful day. The larches, interspersed with autumnal ground cover and evergreen trees, popped vibrantly against the pale blue sky.

We made it to Harts Pass mid-morning, and with the sun properly shining now took the opportunity to dry out our tents before setting off on the final push to the border. We all walked together, chatting happily. And then we started to come across PCT hikers who’d tagged the terminus and were now almost done with the 30-mile stretch back to Harts. Vibes on all sides were high; we were excited to be nearing the end, while those heading back were clearly relieved to be almost done and on their way to civilisation.

I was glad we’d waited out the weather; the mountains were gorgeous once again. A light layer of snow remained in the shadows of the peaks, in the little spaces that never saw sun. We crested Woody Pass just before sunset and were treated to stunning golden hour views of far-off mountain ranges.

Not long afterwards we ran into a group of hikers we knew who had just tagged the terminus. Catching up with them was great fun, although it did put us behind schedule. The sun was sinking rapidly. We pushed on quickly, but progress soon stalled when we arrived at a ridgeline where the blazing orange sun was setting to our left, and a glowing moon was rising on our right. How could we not stop and take it in? It did mean that our last 30 minutes or so descending to Hopkins Lake were in the dark, but it had been worth it. We’d heard rumours that a lot of people were already camped there, and that tent sites were scarce. But we found enough pitches for the five of us pretty quickly, and went to bed feeling like kids the night before Christmas.

📍 Mile 2,636.2 | 🥾 44.58 km | ⛰️ +1,666m / -1,731m

Today was the big day: after four and a half months, and hiking well over the 2,650 miles the trail officially covers (thanks to all our alternates and side quests), we were finally going to reach Canada! It was only 7 miles away. But after we reached the border, we’d have to begin the 30-mile backtrack to Harts Pass; sadly, walking into Canada is no longer allowed. So we set off at 7am as usual, planning to enjoy our time at the terminus, while hopefully still getting some good miles in this afternoon. As we left camp, a pika meeped at us. We took it as a blessing from the trail gods to continue.

The trail was a pretty gentle downhill for the first four miles. We alternated between comfortable silence and brief chats, pausing only once: to pretend to be bears in front of a wildlife camera. Then we arrived at a 3 mile section of blowdowns that had been much fearmongered on FarOut. We thought the rumours must have been overblown, but the deadfall turned out to be kind of gnarly. On the rest of the PCT the blowdowns have at least had their limbs sawed off, but these ones hadn’t been given that treatment and tough branches poked everywhere. I was trying to be careful not to scratch my legs again – I’d done enough of that in NorCal – but in the end I did manage to crack my patella into a branch, right over the top of an old scab from NorCal. It hurt pretty badly for a few seconds, but at least I’d look hardcore in our terminus photo.

We arrived at the top of a short series of switchbacks, and caught our first glimpse of a line of felled trees in the dense forest: that was the border. We could hear other people already at the terminus celebrating. This was it! Just as we finished the last switchback and were on the home stretch Sabretooth, who’d been in the lead, suddenly stopped. She started combing through her pack. We all realised why: we’d picked up a wooden clothespeg at Mazama and had been secretly hiding it in each others’ gear over the last few days. Whoever had it on them at the terminus would have to do a shoey. Out of someone else’s shoe. Satisfied that it wasn’t on her, Sabretooth picked up her bag and we charged towards the terminus, where we were greeted with cheers from the hikers already there.

The other hikers were already preparing to head out, so we wasted no time making them our photographers for group photos at the terminus. As well as a couple of videos of us first popping bubbles, and then doing shoeys. We did a play-by-play of the peg’s movements and discovered that it was with Catch. He took his punishment shoey well. It was only when the hustle and bustle finally died down that we took a seat and had time to take it in. It was a huge accomplishment, and yet it didn’t feel real. Or like the end. It did feel absolutely freezing. We were clearly in a katabatic zone – I’d been perfectly warm when we left camp this morning.

We spent about two hours there, enjoying each other’s company and that of a couple more hikers who arrived shortly after we did. But at the two hour mark the cold really started to get to us, and we prepared to leave. “Don’t you want to hear my speech?” Catch asked. I couldn’t believe I’d forgotten. We’d been badgering him for days to prepare a motivational speech for us. He climbed atop the terminus and we all looked up at him expectantly. Then he began to recite the lyrics to Miley Cyrus’s ‘The Climb’, with a couple of small changes to make it more appropriate: “It kinda was about how fast we got there / It kinda was about what’s waiting on the other side”.

We left in good spirits – the early morning alcohol probably helped with that – and began the climb back up to Hopkins Lake. We synched up playback of our hype playlist, which helped move us along. The pika meeped at us once again as we passed, which we took as a good sign. At the lake we paused for lunch, but not for long. The day had started with a beautiful blue sky, but had turned overcast, cold and windy.

It still didn’t feel quite real that we were done. Probably because we were still hiking. It was nice to have a few miles to walk and reflect and ease ourselves out of trail life. But we all agreed it would’ve been nice if this 30-mile section had been at least 10 miles shorter.

We crossed paths with hikers heading up to the terminus and made sure to fist bump them and cheer them on. Then we started running into familiar faces we hadn’t seen since NorCal, which was a nice surprise. But it meant that we arrived at the campsite we’d chosen in the dark, since we’d spent so much time chatting.

📍 Mile 2,625.2 | 🥾 22.85 km | ⛰️ +815m / -714m

There were only 11 miles between us and our final steps on the PCT. But rain was forecast, and we were keen to get out of it ASAP, so we set off at 7am as usual. The miles practically flew by as we chatted easily all morning, planning all the food we were going to eat now that trail was over. It drizzled lightly, on and off, and the clouds hung low around us so views were non-existent. We spotted a pair of hikers ahead of us and made it our mission to overtake them, which we finally accomplished just before we arrived at a trailhead. We decided to walk the road from there back to Harts Pass, since it would make for faster progress.

Just as we arrived at Harts and signed the last trail log, the rain really started to fall. We’d hoped the ranger would be in so we could call for a ride – there was no mobile service – but we were out of luck. There was only one car in the parking lot, and in this weather we didn’t hold too much hope for getting a hitch from it. So, since a note on the ranger’s door said there was service at a campsite a mile or so away, we decided to head there. It was better than sitting still and growing increasingly cold and wet in the rain.

Arriving at the campsite, though, none of us had any usable signal. Luckily, some day hikers there offered to let us use their phone; but we couldn’t get through to anyone. They said they could probably squeeze a couple of us in when they finished their hike, which we were very grateful for. We also had a lovely surprise, running into a group of hikers we knew well: in fact, it was Shakedown and Sabretooth’s earlier trail family. We spent a good while catching up, but standing still I grew increasingly cold, and eventually had to say goodbye so I could get moving to warm up.

Thankfully, Shakedown managed to convince some other people out for a day hike to allow us all to squeeze into their sedan. The driver turned out to be a volunteer SAR helicopter pilot, so we really lucked out. With three other people and a dog already in the car, though, it was a tight squeeze and we had to surrender our packs to the weather, strapping them to the roof racks. I shivered the whole way down the mountain, cold from the wind and rain. When the driver mentioned they’d been planning to stop at the Mazama Bakery for a coffee, we encouraged the break and gratefully paid for their coffees and ordered our own.

Not long afterwards we were being dropped at the doorstep of the Airbnb we’d booked in Winthrop, where we left our packs and went in search of food. And a celebratory beer, of course. Then we headed to the supermarket to grab some supplies for the next couple of days in town, before making ourselves at home in the Airbnb. Too lazy to cook, dinner was an easy spread of cheese and biscuits, as we cosied up in front of the fireplace to watch movies, introducing Shakedown to the delights of the Twilight franchise.

We slept in as long as our body clocks would allow, and then cooked a delicious big fry up for breakfast. It was a gorgeous, warm, blue-sky day outside, so I went for a bit of a wander around town to take advantage and keep my legs moving at least a little. When I got back we had a lunch of tomato soup and grilled cheese – which we’d fantasised about yesterday.

Then we began a room-to-room beer crawl, which we’d also dreamed up yesterday. Catch kicked us off with another motivational speech – this time, the Aussie classic, ‘Get on the Beers’ by Mashton Kutcher. In the end we only moved between the outdoor space at the front of the house, and the outdoor space at the back, since it was such a nice day it felt wrong to be inside. Slow and steady was definitely the name of the game, and we made it to dinnertime with plenty of beer to spare. As all good dinners should, we started with dessert: s’mores – my first ever, but certainly not my last. Dinner was some easy, delicious homemade pizzas, and we settled into the couch once more, to continue the Harry Potter marathon we’d started at White Pass.

This morning was much the same as yesterday morning – a relative sleep in, a fry up for breakfast – but the air was tinged with a little sadness. Today was our last day together as a group. When we’d finished breakfast and had packed up, reluctant to say goodbye just yet we headed down the main street to grab a coffee, chatting about which book would be our next book club pick, and trying to figure out where and when we could do a reunion hike.

At midday, though, it was time to go our separate ways. Shakedown and Sabretooth were heading to Vancouver, to continue their big year of travel. Catch was going with them, to catch a flight home for a family event. Sass and I were heading to Leavenworth, and then who knows where, as we passed a week waiting for Catch to meet us in Bend – the three of us were going back to fill in the miles we’d missed when we skipped around the smoke from the Austin fire. We hugged goodbye for now, and split in different directions.

Sass and I headed out of town and tried to hitch. Our backup plan was the bus, but it didn’t arrive for a couple of hours. We got lucky quickly: a pickup offered to take us to Twisp. We discovered that there was an earlier bus we could take from there, which connected conveniently with other buses all the way to Leavenworth. We decided to take it; neither of us had the energy to chat with hitches for a couple of hours. We wanted some time to be sad and morose about finishing the trail and saying goodbye to our friends.

The buses ran smoothly and we were dropped in Leavenworth in the late afternoon. There were lots of events on in town this weekend – including Oktoberfest, which was half the reason we’d come – so we made our way to the KOA in the hopes they’d still have a section for PCT hikers. We were in luck, and soon had our tents set up. Then we wandered into town to take advantage of the free beer Icicle Brewing offered to PCT hikers, and enjoyed people watching for a while before heading back to the campsite for an early night.

#8372. Montana Man Banned From Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull

Published Nov 2, 2026 6:36 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A father and son who pleaded guilty to poaching in central Montana have lost their hunting privileges for a combined 24 years. Their poaching activity goes back years, but the investigation into the men started last year based on a tip from two bowhunters, who reported a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery season in September 2025.

“Lawful hunters are some of the most passionate outdoorsmen and women in existence. They’re very quick to report wildlife crimes and violations they see in the field,” Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks game warden and lead investigator Diego O’Brien tells Outdoor Life. “These two individuals, in my opinion, went above and beyond reporting the violation. They were very proactive with assistance in an area that I didn’t know very well. They proved to be incredible resources for me.”

Based on information provided by the two bowhunters, law enforcement located Billings resident Michael Letasky through a traffic stop. He matched the description of the man shooting the bull in the Little Belt Mountains, but he didn’t have the rack or any game meat. The bull was left to waste. (The two witnesses knew exactly where the dead animal was, but by then it was too late for wardens to salvage the meat.)

“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” O’Brien said in a statement. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation. They sacrificed their own hunting trip to ensure justice was served.”

The poached 6×6 bull met the state’s trophy standards. By state code, restitution for the illegal killing and possession or waste of trophy elk is $8,000. The only animal with a higher restitution than a 6×6 bull is a bighorn ram with at least three-fourths curl, which earns a penalty of $30,000.

In addition to the poached bull, Letasky also shot a raghorn with a firearm during the 2023 archery season, and he had an unreported black bear. During the investigation, wardens also found evidence against Letasky’s son, Kolton, of Austin, Texas.

Kolton Letasky killed a Montana buck in 2024 and a Montana bull in 2022 without the proper permits. He pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game and two counts of hunting without a license. His penalties include more than $3,000 in fines and no hunting for four years.

Read Next: YouTuber Poaching Bust Was a Case of ‘Wildlife Commercialization with a Modern Twist,’ Says Investigating Warden

The elder Letasky’s penalties are more severe. Michael Letasky plead guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game, two counts of hunting during a closed season and one count of wasting game. He owes more than $12,000 in fines and can’t hunt for 20 years.

#8370. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8367. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8366. Secrets for Deer Hunting the Big Woods, According to a North Country Expert

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Hunting whitetails in the North Country forests of New England and the Upper Midwest is an undeniably challenging pursuit. Up there the landscapes are massive, think tens of thousands of acres of forest. Food sources and deer sign are more subtle. There are no edges of agricultural fields to target, and there might not even be stands of oaks dropping acorns. Lastly, deer densities are low, with some areas having maybe five deer per square mile.

It’s within this environment that Brett Joy, a member of the Just Hunt Club, has made a name for himself. Using a mix of old-school and modern hunting strategies, Joy has found success killing mature big woods bucks season after season.

I sat down with him for the most recent episode of the Outdoor Life podcast to learn his strategies for targeting mature bucks in the northwoods. Even if you don’t hunt big woods deer yourself, you can learn from Joy’s tactics and experience.

Joy uses digital maps to identify areas where two or three types of habitat converge.

“Whitetails, whether they’re in a cornfield in Iowa or on a mountain in New Hampshire, are edge habitat creatures,” Joy says. “They live on the edges, but those edges can look a lot different depending on where you are in the whitetails’ range.”

In the big woods, look for edges between hardwoods and softwoods, swamps and mature timber, mature timber and early successional growth (recently logged areas). Once you’ve identified these spots, scout them in person. Ideally, you’ll be a mile or more away from any road.

Joy believes that because the habitat is so vast in the big woods, bucks tend to have larger home ranges and core areas. They also have a variety of bedding areas — even in the early season. Whereas in the agricultural country, mature bucks tend to have only a couple woodlots and thickets where they like to bed.

“Our deer could bed on any different point of a mountain in any cut, in a swamp on any given day,” Joy says. “[Those bedding areas] could be miles apart day to day. They’re almost more of a nomadic deer … but they do have areas that they come back to year after year.”

The key is that even if you’re in a buck’s core zone, you might not see him for a week or more.

Like everywhere else in whitetail country, during the rut big woods bucks will travel between doe groups searching for does in estrus.

“But here, you may have only three does that live within 500 acres,” Joy says. So bucks have to cover more ground and do more checking. And this need to travel long distances makes rutting bucks more vulnerable.

“I like to hunt them during the rut and really focus on those areas they frequent when they’re traveling from A to B, or I hunt near one of those doe groups … and if you can find a big primary scrape or pinch point within the core area of those does, you can catch bucks going through there semi-consistently.”

Trail cameras are a critical component of Joy’s strategy because there’s essentially no visibility in the areas that he hunts. In other words, there are not places to glass from in the big woods.

“If I cared less about what buck I was targeting, I could hunt sign and not use cameras and be successful, but I really do rely on them heavily for my strategy,” he says.

Joy positions most of his cameras on large community scrapes because they serve as social gathering spots that will attract deer in vast landscapes. On top of that, Joy focuses on secluded, high-elevation areas that bucks tend to prefer.

Joy aims to run cameras from about October 15 through December 15, which gives him the full range of rut activity.

When you’re hunting the rut in the big woods, you need to have a good understanding of peak rut activity dates.

“What dictates everything is does coming into estrus,” Joy says. “And those bucks absolutely know those dates in this landscape and they will show up checking those doe groups on the same few days year after year.”

Joy conducted an in-depth trail camera survey using several years worth of his trail camera photos, plus his buddy’s photos to identify peak deer activity during the rut. He found that peak activity in his area was November 19th.

He then paired his trail cam data data with a biologist’s data on fawn conception dates in New Hampshire and he found that the peak conception date was November 19 as well.

“If I had to pick five or seven days, I’d put November 19th right in the middle of it,” Joy says.

Joy adds that he hasn’t witnessed a shutdown in activity due to lockdown. Bucks are covering the most ground during daylight during peak breeding dates.

But peak activity is different throughout whitetail country. You must examine your own trail camera photos and examine historical data to nail down the key dates where you hunt.

Read Next: North Woods Legend Hal Blood on Snow Tracking Bucks

“Now to kill deer in these landscapes you can’t just expect to hunt one weekend,” Joy says. You need probably a week of hunting and you need to hunt for the entire week, dark to dark, he says.

Joy will set up different stands within an area for different wind directions, but once he picks an area he sticks with it and does not jump around from spot to spot — even if he’s not seeing deer right away.

“Sometimes I don’t make a decision about where I’m going to sit until the day before … I’ll wait until I have all the information on a particular spot, but once I decide to [hunt there], that’s it. There’s no deviating. Once you start to doubt and jump around, you’re done,” Joy says. “The day you’re not there is the day he’ll come by.”

If you have good trail camera data and historical data on a spot, it makes it easier to commit to it for a week of hunting. Other keys to staying in the hunt long-term are: efficient access to your stand, good clothing to keep you warm, quality food to eat throughout the week, plenty of rest at night, and staying hydrated. Most importantly, you’ve got to keep the faith.

“Sitting in the cold for 11 or 12 hours a day, day after day, it really does wear on you and you start to doubt yourself and doubt your spot. You start to become negative, and once that stuff compounds … you’re not going to be there when that buck comes by.”

If you are able to stay patient and stick it out, there’s a good chance that an old northwoods buck will eventually walk by. And no matter how big his rack is, he’ll be a true trophy whitetail.

#8363. Zero In Newton, NJ

I satisfy my cravings for town food and financial planning. I witness sports history.

What does a Trek blogger do with a free morning? The answer is…tax planning. Seriously. Personal finance is something of a hobby of mine. I had an idea while hiking during the week and wanted to model it and see the impact on my future tax liability. Riveting stuff, lemme tell ya.

While I had my nose buried in a spreadsheet I had one eye on the replay of yesterday’s F1 qualifying session for the Mexico City Grand Prix. Later in the day I could focus on the race itself which proved eventful. When the dust had settled, Formula One had its 2026 champion in Kimi Antonelli. Kimi stepped up in just his second season with a quixotic campaign to become the youngest ever Formula One champion. He is Italy’s first champion in 73 years. His championship is unquestionably well-deserved as he accumulated his large lead while dueling with 4 other F1 world champions, and shared this weekend’s podium with 2 of them in an incredible moment of serendipity. I won’t soon forget this season both for the unlikely champion and for having watched it while hiking the Appalachian Trail (and while writing this blog).

I celebrated Kimi’s title with unlimited soda refills, pizza, and ice cream, as is my usual M.O. The cafe gave me a peppermint mocha free of charge! I can’t say its something I’d order, I tend to stick to the basics with everything, including coffee, but I’ll admit it was pretty tasty.

I spent some time putting together a viable itinerary for the remainder of my hike. The plan gives me one day of buffer and an end date of November 22nd, assuming I take it easy over 3 days to complete the 4 state challenge during the southbound leg to be well rested to attempt to make the return trip northbound in a single day. Lately I’ve been wondering if I should record some video to document the attempt. It isn’t something I’ve done before, but this is certainly a year of firsts!

The Peppermint Mocha, tastes like the holidays.

Incredible. I now have less than 500 miles of hiking left to complete my journey. When I started out, I wasn’t sure it was possible. I had countless ideas to hike most of the trail by skipping sections if I didn’t feel up to the task. It doesn’t look like those will be necessary now.

It was a little bit of an up and down week. Tuesday felt like a new low after twisting my increasingly sensitive ankle several times. No worries though – its probably either a bruise or a slight stretch of the tendon. My ankles have survived years of hiking without feeling so much as a pinch. They are as strong as ever, just meeting their match on the slippery rocks this time of year.

Depending on where you draw the line, I officially completed New York either on Thursday or Saturday. The NY/NJ line I documented on Thursday is not the first time the trail enters New York heading northbound, it first enters New York shortly after the New Jersey high point, but soon crosses back into New Jersey and back again several times. I don’t think it is a coincidence that the AT follows the state line closely, it is likely the result of that stretch of land being public.

I also semi-retired my first pair of Altra Olympus 6 shoes that I put on at the start of the White Mountains since they have now accumulated 1,000 miles. They seem to have plenty of life left, they will accrue more miles on future hikes for sure.

Welcome to November, its finishing month! The time change will be welcome, I feel lazy waiting for the sun to come up to start hiking only to realize that it is already 8:00AM by the time I actually make it onto the trail. The time change won’t bring any more daylight, it will be startling to see daylight running out before 5:00PM.

My first 2-day stint will see me finish all but about 1 mile of New Jersey. I’ll be crossing the Delaware Water Gap on Wednesday and setting foot in Pennsylvania for the first time since mid-July. There are warmer days ahead, but also a chance of rain later in the week. Rocks are guaranteed, northern Pennsylvania is infamous for them. We’ll see if their reputation is warranted.

#8362. The FN Mauser Is the Best Deer Rifle that History Forgot

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Hunting rifles come and go and sometimes even good ones don’t stay around. The decades following World War II saw a boom in hunters and a voracious appetite for new rifles and cartridges. This was the heyday of the Pre-64 Model 70 and the Winchester Magnums, but we no longer hear much about the many Mauser sporting rifles made by FN and imported from Belgium.

I recently got my mitts on one of these rifles, which belonged to my great grandfather, chambered in .270 Win. While this gun undoubtedly rode around in the rifle rack of Grandpa Curtis’s truck when I was a youngster, I’m looking at it anew. According to my dad and uncle, Grandpa’s brother was a gunsmith and built the rifle for him. This was after he’d raised a family in a log cabin in Colorado during the Depression and developed a taste for July mule deer. He used this rifle to shoot a lot of deer and elk.

A family heirloom like this gives me a perspective on what a quality hunting rifle looked like in the 1950s, and an idea of how well it’s held up over time. It’s also fun to compare it to the rifles we have today.

It’s common to hear or read about the many sporterized military rifles that post-war hunters adopted. These would typically be either 1903 Springfields or remnant military Mauser rifles. But these FN Mausers weren’t sporterized — they were manufactured for a couple decades as sporting-specific guns. Many, including this rifle, were imported by Firearms International Corp. and marked as such on the receivers.

They were brought in and sold by various companies and in numerous formats. An ad in the November, 1951 Issue of Outdoor Life displays the JC Higgins Model 50 — which was simply an FN Mauser and sold at Sears, Roebuck. They had the chrome vanadium steel barrel and even came with a 2.5-power scope, for $135. Another ad, from the September, 1952 issue, for the Parker-Whelen Gun Catalog, lists .30/06 and .270 FN Mausers for $137.50 without a receiver-mounted rear sight. That would cost you another ten bucks. This could be a clue to the specific origin of this .270, as the front of the barrel has markings that appear to be where a front sight was once mounted, but there is no evidence of a barrel-mounted rear sight like you’ll see on Pre-64 Model 70 rifles and others like the Remington Model 721.

Ultimately, lots of these guns were imported in various forms and were sold by companies like Weatherby, Harrington & Richardson, and Colt. Complete FN rifles, according to what little I could find, had a specific pearl edge to the checkering on the grips, but it’s likely that not all of them did. Barrelled actions were also imported and built into custom hunting rifles.

This particular rifle appears to be either one that showed up as a barrelled action — possibly with a front sight. The barrel and receiver both bear the appropriate stampings for a matched pair that left the factory in Belgium. But the 22-inch barrel appears to have been cut down and re-crowned — as these were generally 24-inch barrels. It’s stamped with the year “1951” and bears matching 2837 serial numbers.

The stock has a handsome grain and good ergonomics. It lacks any checkering, but the fore-end has a nice belly and is capped with an ivory-colored plastic cap. The grip is capped with a similar plastic cap and its vertical orientation provides a wonderful balance of trigger reach and allows a crisp perpendicular squeeze. The raised comb is, in part, made from a separate block of wood. It’s pinned atop the buttstock and shaped to match, but the seams are still visible.

The floorplate isn’t hinged on this rifle. Rather, it’s detachable and retained by a spring-loaded button at the rear and retaining lip at the front. The fitting of the stock is very precise and, despite being bedded from the tang to the cap on the fore-end, very little bedding material is visible alongside the metal. Pillars around the action screws also help create an incompressible bridge between the bottom metal and action. The precise fit of metal and wood are things we’ll only see today on custom rifles and the highest-end production guns. Factory stocks — both wood and synthetic — are either CNC-milled or molded with baked-in tolerances rather than hand fit. The workmanship on my 1954 Model 70 is good, but not to the same level.

The barrel is a pretty standard sporter taper, finishing at .635 inches. I assume it has been cut down from 24 inches to 22. It’s a heavier barrel than you’ll see on classics like the M70 featherweight and contributes to the rifle’s roughly 9.5-pound overall weight.

The action and barrel share all matching and appropriate proof marks, and remain in good shape, with the bolt sliding like glass down the slick raceways. The bottom of the bolt handle is flattened and knurled for a better grip, and is generally smoother to operate than my previously mentioned M70. The safety switch is textured on both sides. It appears to be pitting because of its irregularity, but no other parts show similar signs of corrosion.

The receiver is topped with a one-piece Redfield mount and Bear Cub 2 ¾-power scope that uses a post-style reticle. In the early days of magnified optics, this gave a sight picture similar to that of a front post iron sight — to which most shooters would be accustomed. It was fitted with a Canjar trigger — a premium aftermarket upgrade, that breaks at 3 pounds, 7 ounces as set.

To test the rifle for accuracy, I fired four five-shot groups with several different types of contemporary .270 ammo. Where we would normally aggregate these five-shot groups into a single 20-shot group for each type of ammo, It was apparent that the system was limited, in part, by the optic, so I’m just sticking with the group size averages.

I believe the rifle is certainly capable of better accuracy than this but, considering the vintage scope, it proved itself perfectly capable of hitting a deer or elk cleanly out to 200 to 300 yards. Frankly, it’s not uncommon for us to test modern rifles with high-magnification scopes that average worse. A low-power optic itself doesn’t prevent a rifle from shooting accurately either, but this style of reticle requires the correct-sized target and a lot of concentration to maintain a consistent hold. The post covers about four inches of a 100-yard target. When the barrel warmed, mirage definitely affected sight picture too. I tried both a six-o’clock hold and a navy hold (dead center), and saw some vertical stringing with both methods.

Read Next: 10 Classic Hunting Rifles Every Hunter Should Own

For as much as we hear about classic rifles like the Savage 99 and Winchester Model 70, I’m surprised that Mausers like this haven’t carried a similar reputation. So many rifles, including the Winchester, were derived from the Mauser action itself. The rifles even commanded a higher price than Model 70s at the time. While precision manufacturing, materials, and coatings have gotten better, a rifle like this one could still hold its own today.

#8360. Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni

#8358. Day 20/21 – An Unexpected Party

Route: Pennine Way thru-hike – Kirk Yetholm, out and back

After all the trains and buses, and pleasant days wandering around towns and cities in the northeastern UK, I arrived in Kirk Yetholm.  The Border Hotel, the official end of the Pennine Way was just as warm and cozy as I imagined.  It was with a certain amount of melancholy that I found myself standing on the village green of this tiny settlement in Scotland.  Signs posted at the terminus of the trail allowed me to reminisce the points along my own journey.

Per tradition, the folks at the pub offered me a free half pint to commemorate my arrival.  I declined.  I had not earned that reward.

My room was lovely and comfortable with a view of the garden.  I had made this reservation months ago.  My two boxes had arrived a couple of weeks earlier and were waiting for me in my room.  In hindsight, I should have left the extra clothes at home.  Everything in those two boxes now needed to fit in my pack.  This included a large duffel that I use to protect my backpack when checked for the flight.

The rest of the day passed quietly.  Tomorrow, Graeme and Rachel would arrive at the end of their Pennine Way walk.

The next morning, after breakfast, I decided I could at least have a look around.  With my ankle brace and the last 10 days of recovery, I could comfortably walk 3 or 4 miles.  A walk around town revealed that Kirk Yetholm has no shops or cafes.  It is literally the hotel, a church, and the nearby houses and pastures.  Residents use the bus to Kelso in order to shop.  There was nothing left but the trail.

In total, I had walked 117.5 miles on the Pennine Way.  If I walked another 3 miles, I could round out my achievement to 120 miles.  And so, off I went.  Skies were grey, but there didn’t look to be any rain.  I headed out of town, south on the Pennine Way, just me and my hiking boots.  No pack.

The road out of the village climbs steeply, past sheep and pony pastures.  Then it descends to a fork: the “high road” and the “low road”.  The lower path continued on the paved road. The high road headed into the open hills.  My spirit needed the high road.  I turned left, crossed a small stream, and headed upwards.

As I climbed, the wind grew stronger.  It was literally pushing me up the slope!  By the time I reached the top of the rise at Green Humbleton, I had to lean into the wind to remain standing.  But I didn’t care.  This is where I wanted to be.  This hilltop was just about 2 miles from Kirk Yetholm.  This would do.  I turned around to head back.

Afterwards, I spent some time relaxing in my room before heading to the pub for a cider.  I was about halfway through my beverage when Graeme and Rachel walked in, followed by a large entourage!  Although they live in the US, they are originally from the UK with lots of friends remaining in their home country.  And all those friends joined them for the last section of the Pennine.

It was such a festive evening.  Graeme and Rachel were celebrated by the landlord of the inn, who stopped by to tell us the history of the place and share his favorite jokes.  The official register, going back to 1968, was signed and certificates were handed out.  They had done it!  I was so happy for them.

The next few hours were full of food, drink, and fellowship.  Everyone shared stories.  The landlord eventually sent over a round of Limoncello!  We were there past closing, but it was finally time to say farewell.  Both to new friends and to the Pennine Way.  Tomorrow, I would backtrack my way via buses and trains to Edinburgh where I would await my flight home.

I went to see a podiatrist as soon as I returned home.  The first thing he told me was, “ligaments take longer to heal than bones.”

Exactly one month before I started the Pennine Way, I was making the long, rocky descent from Furnace Mountain in Shenandoah National Park.  I had been wilderness backpacking for three days.  With less than three miles left in my trip, I rolled my left ankle—badly!  I took a long break and did my best at some trailside first aid.

That injury came back to haunt me.  The doctor explained that my ankle had not yet fully healed, even though I had no pain  It eventually gave out due to overuse.  It took me 100 miles to hit that threshold, but once it gave out, there was nothing to do but secure it in a brace and get off the trail.  The good news is that I can expect a full recovery.  As of yesterday, he said I can run and hike again as long as I wear my brace for the next month and don’t experience any pain.

I’ve decided to write one last post, consolidating my lessons-learned and talking about overall costs.  If that sounds fun or useful, join me for that final post.  And thank you one and all for the kind comments and encouragement as I pursued my Pennine Way dreams.

#8356. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

With no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

The paddling portion went quickly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”

Using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They also effectively halved the 480km trek by packrafting over two large lakes, including Nettilling, the world’s largest lake on an island. Yet there was no way to ease the final 160km slog into Iqaluit.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8355. A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:09 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Robert Denninger was in a tree saddle the afternoon of October 23 when he spotted a deer in a creek bed about 75 yards away. He’d accessed the Oklahoma public hunting area by kayak, paddling up a creek to a remote spot that he’d pinpointed the previous day.

“I decided to slide down quietly with my bow and get a better look at the deer in the creek,” Denninger tells Outdoor Life. “When I got close to the creek I spotted two big mature bucks fighting and they were locked up tight by their antlers.”

He knew he was witnessing an epic outdoor event and he shot video of the fight on his phone.

“The bucks were plowing into each other and into the creek bank,” says Denninger, a 42-year-old retiree from Dallas. “Mud was flying everywhere. My mind was racing – would attempting to harvest these bucks be a hunter’s gift or a violation of fair chase?”

It was clear the bucks were not able to separate their antlers. Denninger struggled with what to do and pondered if it would be ethical and legal to shoot the larger of the two bucks, which was a 12-pointer with a typical rack. He recalled a friend telling him a story of once finding a pair of locked-antler bucks dead in a pond. They had been killed and half eaten by coyotes.

Before deciding what to do, Denninger called a game warden.

“I spoke with a local [Oklahoma] Game Warden who assured me he didn’t have any on-call vet who could have come out to sedate the animals and attempt a safe unlocking,” Denninger says.

“The thought of letting ‘nature run its course’ and coming back in the following days to spook a pack of coyotes off two rotten carcasses or trying my best to put an ethical kill on these animals were what I believed my choices were,” he explains. “I decided to shoot the 12-pointer.”

His first arrow was deflected by brush. But his second arrow found the deer’s heart, and it quickly died.

“I watched to see if the eight point could free himself, but he only struggled more, barely able to move the weight of the harvested 12-pointer,” the bowhunter says.

Denninger had no way of freeing the deer, so he decided to shoot the second buck with his bow. Even when both deer were dead, it was impossible to unlock their antlers.

That’s when he called a couple younger buddies, who eventually arrived with a wheeled wagon.

“We tried to unlock their racks many times, and were unable to,” Denninger says. “We field dressed them. But it was a rugged haul to get the two bucks out, taking well over three hours to get them to a truck and out of the woods. It was almost midnight [by the time we were done].”

He called his Texas friend and taxidermist Dustin Moon and told him about the locked-antler bucks and his hunting tale.

“Dustin and his wife Stephanie of New Story Taxidermy drove five hours (on their sixth wedding anniversary) to where I was so they could see the bucks and help my deer processor get their antlers unlocked.”

Eventually they succeeded and the deer were separated. They will be mounted, though Denninger doesn’t know if he’ll have them in a locked-horn mount or separate mounts.

The 12-pointer is believed to be 7.5 years old and has a rough green score of 152 inches. It’s the biggest buck Denninger has taken during his dedicated bowhunting career. The 8-pointer is thought to be 5.5 years old and scores 132 inches. Both bucks have typical racks.

“I think what I did was the most ethical thing I could have done with my two Oklahoma buck tags, especially considering the alternative of having them suffer and die in their struggle, or have coyotes kill them.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8351. How to Mount a Riflescope Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When mounting a riflescope, you’re dealing with the most fragile and failure-prone point on your gun—so it pays to do it right. The process isn’t complicated, but it does require an attention to detail and some basic equipment. So in part one of our seven-part series on mastering the use of precision riflescopes and shooting to your rifle’s full potential, I’m going to dive in to how to actually get one of these bad boys mounted properly.

To correctly mount a riflescope, these conditions must be satisfied: The reticle needs to be level with the rifle. The scope must be positioned at the correct height above the bore. The proper eye relief needs to be established. And the fasteners in the rings and bases need to be tightened the right way. Before we get into detail on each of these points, here’s a basic outline of the process.

• Clamp the barrel in the padded jaws of a bench vise. If you don’t have a bench vise, you’ll need a solid gun cradle that will hold the rifle steady.

• Use a bubble level to level the rifle action. The flat on top of the Picatinny rail works. With some actions you can remove the bolt and have enough clearance on the tang (assuming it is flat) to set a bubble level as well. As a last resort you can attach the bottom half of a scope ring to the scope base and rest the level on it.

• Set the scope in the rings and lightly tighten the fasteners so that the scope will stay put but can be rotated and moved by hand. If your scope has a flat spot on the elevation turret, place the bubble level on it to level the reticle.

• An alternate method to level the reticle is to look through the scope on your leveled rifle at a plumb bob and orient the vertical crosshair with the string.

• Once the reticle is level, remove the rifle from vise and check your eye relief. Make adjustments as needed. Do this by placing the rifle back in the vise, making sure it is level, and then moving the scope.

• Tighten the fasteners to the correct torque levels with a torque wrench.

The depth of the scope rings controls how far above the bore the scope sits. The primary concern is that both ends of the scope have adequate clearance above the rifle. Having the objective end of the scope in contact with the barrel is an obvious no-no, but you want to make sure the eyepiece isn’t cramped either. Rings that are too low can limit the horizontal travel of the scope in the rings making it more difficult to get the right eye relief.

If your scope is too high, you’ll have a hard time lining up behind the rifle when shooting prone, though a stock with an adjustable cheek piece can mitigate this.

Ultimately, this is a Goldilocks situation where the scope should neither be too high, nor too low. As a rule of thumb, a gap between the objective bell and the barrel of .25 to .5 inches should be just right—but the profile of your barreled action and stock might dictate otherwise.

With proper eye relief the shooter is able to look through the scope without any part of the image being blacked out. The way to test whether eye relief (and scope height) are correct is to get set up behind the rifle in the prone position, close your eyes, rest your check firmly on the stock by taking the tension out of your neck, then opening your eyes.

You should be looking right down the center of the riflescope and have a clear view of the reticle and image without needing to move your head.

Fortunately, many long-range rifles make fine tuning this easier by have adjustable lengths of pull and cheek piece height. Rifles equipped with Picatinny rails—which most precision rifles are—provide greater flexibility with the forward and aft placement of the scope to establish good eye relief.

Read Next: The Best Scope Rings of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Some manufacturers provide values for the fasteners in their scope rings. Many don’t. As a rule of thumb, you can tighten the screws on scope rings to about 20 inch-pounds and be good to go.

It always makes sense to check the screws on your Pic rail or scope base as well. They tend to be beefier, so you can torque them to about 30 inch-pounds without worry.

You can use a torque wrench with preset fittings, like Fix-It Sticks or the Wheeler Fat Wrench, or one with an indicator dial like this one from Seekonk Precision Tools.

Before tightening the screws, you should consider doing one of two things. Either use a sparing amount of blue Loctite on the treads—a single small drop will do—or spray the screws with some degreaser. These will help the screws acquire a more secure hold.

Tighten the screws as you would lug nuts on a truck tire. Tighten one a bit, go to a screw on the other side of the ring and tighten that a bit, and repeat as you work your way through all the fasteners.

Tighten them gradually so that the rings are applying an even clamping force to the scope tube. When done correctly, the gap on either side of the rings should be even. That’s a good sign that whoever put the scope on the rifle knew their stuff.

John B. Snow is Shooting Editor of Outdoor Life, where he oversees the publication’s firearms and shooting coverage. This includes gear reviews, features on technical innovations, stories on shooting techniques and general hunting coverage with the occasional fishing story thrown into the mix.

#8350. Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to quickly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.
