#8271. This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

Published Nov 7, 2026 1:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot. Every day or two it sends you a photo of a giant old buck, and now all you’ve got to do is wait for the right wind to sneak in there and hunt him. And then, all of a sudden, the camera goes dead.

It’s a new camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell? Welcome to the often frustrating world of modern trail camera use.

I’ve been field testing and running trail cameras year-round for several years now and in my experience, there is no camera brand out there that’s immune to malfunctions and failures. But my experience pales in comparison to that of Rich Howell of Trail Cam Pro. Howell has been objectively testing and experimenting with trail cameras for more than 20 years.

I recently interviewed Howell on the Outdoor Life podcast and he shared several reasons why hunters see so many camera failures in the field. Some of it has to do with how we’re using the cameras, and some of it has to do with how the cams are made (which is usually pretty cheaply). Plus, Howell hints at where he thinks the future of trail cameras is headed, and it’s all about making a system that is more affordable and useful to hunters. It’s a conversation worth listening to ahead of the heart of hunting season.

In the meantime, here’s why our cameras often go down in the field, and what we can do to fix them.

Standard alkaline batteries often don’t have the required power to keep a trail camera running reliably, Howell says. If you’re getting fine daytime pictures, but blank, black images at night, it’s a good sign you have a battery issue as there’s not enough power for the camera to fire the flash. This can happen even when the camera is displaying decent battery life.

More expensive lithium batteries can work well, but they too can have issues. Howell noticed that about 1 in 20 lithium batteries would go bad very quickly, (like within days of use) and sometimes this was enough to prevent the camera from working.

Howell now suggests that hunters use rechargeable lithium batteries, which have proven to be more reliable. Having a pool of these batteries on rotation will help solve many trail camera power troubles.

When hunters first jump into the cellular trail camera game, they often like to get their photos sent immediately. In the beginning it’s fun to get a notification and then have that instant gratification of seeing a deer photo.

But it’s usually more effective to have a cell camera batch send images every 12 hours or 24 hours. This is a key way to preserve battery life, and it’s also a more useful way to analyze trail camera data.

Personally, I like to have cameras send every 24 hours and then I review all the cameras everyday in the morning. Looking at all the cameras on the property at once helps me put together activity trends.

Howell says that solar panels definitely can help keep your camera powered, but they often have issues in the field. First, you want to make sure that they are facing south to capture as most sun as possible. This can be a challenge if you want your camera facing north. And second, squirrels have a tendency to chew through solar panel wires. If you’re setting up your camera and panel in the hardwoods, there’s a good chance a squirrel is going to get to it. In other words, solar panels can be a useful tool, but they’re not a silver bullet.

If you’re using the stock camera strap, you’re just asking for trouble. The tag ends of these straps always seem to come loose (triggering the camera) and you’re never able to position the camera perfectly on the tree with them. Plus, other hunters can easily spot the strap, which is an important consideration if you’re hunting public land. Howell suggests using an adjustable tree mount to make sure you can position the camera exactly where it needs to go. You can find a wealth of  trail camera information on the Trail Cam Pro website and by subscribing to their newsletter.

#8269. Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

Published Nov 7, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I had just come back from the service in 1954. My wife was expecting our first baby, and I was running a general store on Highway 97 just outside of Bainbridge, Georgia. Hardly a day went by that someone didn’t come in and tell tales of Old Ripper.

Old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp. That hog tore up more fences, broke more gates, broke the backs of more female hogs and was chased by more hunters than any critter there has ever been in this country. Ripper had been shot by several people. My Daddy fired at him seven times with an M-1 carbine and believed he hit him, but the hog never fell. He had been hunted with dogs and he had killed plenty of dogs. There never was a hog hound that could hold him. The last time the boar was run with hounds, he killed two of the best hounds in the county with his slashing tusks, so no one else ever put their dogs on Old Ripper.

Old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy. Farmers around Bainbridge went to the hardware stores and bought brand-new aluminum gates to put in the gaps he made in their fences. Within a week, the gates were often all bent and torn up where that crazy boar had stuck his nose under and bent them to get into a pasture or field. There was no hog wire or barbed wire fence that could keep Old Ripper out.

That boar was walking destruction. The farmers hated him not only for tearing up fences and gates, but even more because of what he did to their sows. Ripper would break into a pig parlor, tear up the pens and release all the sows. Then he would take them off for a stroll in the woods. Old Ripper weighed 438 pounds. So when he mounted some of the young sows, he broke their backs. Then the sows would have to be destroyed. The sows he did breed threw shoats that were as wild and crazy as he was. The piglets wouldn’t fatten and brought almost nothing at the market.

Everybody was out to get Old Ripper. My dad was accustomed to catching wild hogs. We used to catch them in the Fowltown Swamp, fatten them and sell them at the market. My daddy knew about trapping hogs. He built traps to catch Old Ripper. On two separate occasions Old Ripper did go into one of daddy’s traps, but he tore up the wooden stockades and broke out both times. My daddy wouldn’t stand for that, so daddy got a steel bear trap and set it for Ripper. When daddy went back the next day he found the giant tracks of Old Ripper and followed them to the trap. But instead of catching a renegade hog, he found the bear trap had been sprung by the big boar.

One reason Old Ripper became a legend was his ability to outthink the farmers and the hunters in our area. He had been around humans so much that in many cases he just outthought folks instead of using brute force. The people around our place began to think Old Ripper might be a supernatural creature. He was a boar, but he was a smart boar. No dogs could hold him, no stockades could enclose him, no fence could stop him and no man had been able to kill him for seven years.

Other episodes added to the legend of Old Ripper. One of the meanest things Old Ripper ever did involved Mrs. Ella T. Hand’s daughter-in-law, who was five months pregnant. She was in her kitchen and heard a disturbance out among her sows. She went out to the pig parlor and saw Old Ripper trying to tear the planks off the posts where she had her sows penned up. She picked up a rock and threw it at the old boar to try and run him off. When he saw her, he turned, looked straight at her and charged. Only a few steps away was a giant red oak stump that stood about three feet off the ground. The lady climbed up on the stump and began to scream for her husband. All the while, Old Ripper was going around the stump, snorting and blowing. He attempted to rear up on that stump and get to her but she stayed just out of reach of his razor-sharp tusks. For an hour the hog circled the stump as the lady screamed for help. Finally her husband came home. When he saw what was happening, he grabbed his shotgun from over the fireplace and ran toward the hog. At less than 10 yards, he shot Old Ripper in the side of the head with birdshot. The hog merely shook his head, looked at the man and trotted off.

To say Old Ripper was hated by everybody in the community would be a vast understatement. Every man and boy dreamed of killing that old boar, and plenty of work was forgotten by the men who hunted him. All it took to organize a community hog hunt was for someone to report that they’d seen Old Ripper. Every man and boy within earshot would grab a gun and head for the swamp.

I would have liked to have hunted Old Ripper, but I had mouths to feed. I didn’t have time to waste on that renegade boar. I had just bought a brand-new lever-action Marlin .30/30. I was proud of that gun and took it out behind the store to test it out. On that particular day, Mrs. Ella T. Hand happened to be sitting out in front of the store. Mrs. Hand was close to 80 years old. She always wore a sunbonnet, a long dress and about 90 percent of the time, she had a dip of snuff in her mouth. Mrs. Hand saw me kill a crow sitting in the field about 150 yards away with that rifle. I knew I’d made a lucky shot, but she didn’t. She told everyone for a month about how good I could shoot with that new .30/30.

“If that old wild hog comes back around my sows, I’m going to come and get you, Jack, and let you kill him with that new rifle,” she told me.

Well, about a month later, here comes Mrs. Ella T. in her 1949 pickup truck.

“Jack, that old boar is up in my field with some sows he run off,” she told me. “Now I don’t expect you’ll have any better luck than anybody else who has tried to kill him, but I sure wish you’d bring that new rifle up to the field and give it a try.”

I closed up my little country store and got into the front seat of that pickup truck with Mrs. Ella T. to try my hand at Old Ripper. I had five cartridges with copper-jacketed lead-headed bullets in my gun—the kind that open up but still go on through. There wasn’t any doubt in my mind that if I could hit that boar, the bullets would do the damage needed to put him down.

We drove to Mrs. Hand’s 40-acre peanut field, which backed up to the edge of Fowltown Swamp. I saw Old Ripper out in the middle of the field with four sows he had just broken out from their pen. The five pigs were all rooting in the peanuts. There was a hog wire fence around the field, with barbed wire on the top. The field, which was about 250 yards wide and about twice as long, was on a hillside. Old Ripper and the sows were up close to the top of the hill and I was down near the bottom. There was a dried-up creekbed that ran under the fence. From the tracks in the wash, I figured this was where Old Ripper and the sows had gotten into the field. The creekbed was only about two or three feet deep, but it was big enough for me to crawl under the fence and still stay out of sight. I could lay down in the bottom of the wash, crawl along on my stomach and Old Ripper wouldn’t be able to see me.

Until that day, I had never seen Old Ripper. I had looked at fences he had torn up and I had seen mud on the sides of the trees where he had rubbed. I knew he was a big boar, but I never realized just how big. When I saw Old Ripper standing there in the sun, his black bristles gathered in the rays of light and made him look a deep royal blue. He was a magnificent animal standing about four feet high, and he completely dwarfed the sows following him.

I said to myself, “Doggone your hide, Old Ripper! I’m going to try and get a little closer to you.”

The wash meandered from the bottom of the slope where I was uphill to where Old Ripper was rooting in the peanut patch. Lying flat on my belly, I would crawl for 10 yards and then peep over the edge to see where Old Ripper was. Each time I looked, the old boar was about 10 yards farther from the place than he had been before. It was just like he had a sixth sense that warned him of danger. He kept the same distance away, about 230 yards from me, from the time I first saw him until I decided to shoot. After I had crawled 30 yards, Old Ripper and his band of runaway sows were within 10 yards of a thick broom sedge field. I knew that if he got into that field, I wouldn’t be able to see to shoot him.

The wash was shallower and just barely kept me out of the boar’s view. The shot had to be over 200 yards. So I laid the rifle down on the lip of the wash, looked through the open sights and aimed at the top of Old Ripper’s shoulder. When I squeezed off the first shot, I saw the dust fly off the boar’s shoulder and heard the bullet make a dull thud when it hit him, but Old Ripper showed no sign of being wounded.

Then I stood up. Old Ripper reared up on his hind legs and bellowed like a wild bull. The hair on the back of my neck stood up. I had caught or killed more than 100 hogs out of that swamp, but I had never heard a hog make a sound like that.

When Old Ripper came down on his front feet, he was on a dead run, headed right down that hill. I knew that when he got to the bottom of the hill, he had business with me. I should have killed Old Ripper with that first shot, but he was far from dead. I didn’t panic. I knew that before the boar got to me, I would have time to fire four more of those .30/30 shells. I thought there was no way I wouldn’t kill him before he got to me. I had faced other wild hogs before.

With every shot, I believed I was pumping more lead into Old Ripper, but he never slowed. He still came on toward me. I took my time, aimed, squeezed, heard the report of the rifle, jacked another shell into the chamber and fired again. I knew I was hitting the boar, but he never missed a stride.

When Old Ripper was less than 50 yards away, I heard the hammer fall on an empty chamber. That was the loudest, most desperate sound I ever heard in my life.

I looked around and saw one lone cherry tree with no limbs on it about 30 yards to my right, but my feet wouldn’t work. I knew I couldn’t stay where I was, but I couldn’t go anywhere else. Old Ripper just kept on coming. I finally threw that gun down and began to run. Then I saw Old Ripper, now 20 yards away, running on two crippled front legs. I knew then that I had a chance to outrun him, but just as that idea went through my mind, the big boar fell and rolled to a stop about 10 yards away from me. He never moved, he never grunted and he never made another sound.

There was a slight breeze coming from that dead boar to me. Old Ripper’s odor was the strongest, rankest smell I ever have smelled. It was awful. I waited awhile to make sure Old Ripper was dead. Then I looked to see where my bullets had hit. The first had entered the shoulder. The second went through the hog’s loin and had gone into his stomach. Two other shots had hit his fore shoulders and entered the chest cavity. One bullet just flat-out missed.

Looking at Old Ripper, I was kind of sad that he was gone. Even if he was a renegade, he was a magnificent animal. There had never been a boar like him before that I ever heard tell of, and there never was another.

Mrs. Ella T.’s son James and her husband Ressie helped me load Old Ripper onto the pickup truck. We took the boar to Mr. Smoke Roger’s platform scales at Fayetteville, Georgia. The boar tipped the scales at 438 pounds. We struggled to reload the boar and then drove back to Bainbridge. Dr. Cooper, the veterinarian at that time, examined him. Below Ripper’s inch-thick hide was a sheath of gristle that extended from his huge shoulders to the middle of his back. This sheath had been Old Ripper’s armor and had turned the shotgun pellets and rifle bullets over the years. Dr. Cooper said the boar was between 8 and 10 years old and was probably a throwback to some of the European wild boars let loose in this country years before.

Read Next: I’ve Been Charged by Bears and Moose. Wild Hogs Are Much, Much Worse

When my daddy saw that the boar filled up the bed of that pickup truck, he could hardly believe his eyes. He had wanted to be the one who killed Old Ripper, but since he didn’t, he was glad it was me.

“That ol’ hog has cost farmers in this area thousands of dollars and many good sows, as well as being responsible for a lot of little pigs that weren’t fit to sell,” my daddy said. “I’m glad he’s gone.”

Since then the old Fowltown Swamp where Old Ripper used to roam and where wild pigs lived and bred for hundreds of years has vanished. Old Ripper’s haunts are covered by Lake Seminole today, but I remember it like it was when that boar was less than 30 yards away on a dead run bringing hurt to me, and I heard the sound of the hammer on my .30/30 falling on an empty chamber.

#8267. Intro

Organizing camp is one of the great pleasures of backpacking, and the behaviors behind it are fundamentally encoded in our brains.

In the fall of 2025, under banner-blue skies, I backpacked into a remote Utah canyon to help celebrate my friend Ace’s birthday. The highlight was a hundred-foot natural arch, located at a widening in the gulch, where there was enough room for the ten of us (and five giddy dogs) to spread out and set up our camps with fantastic views of the span and enough distance to smother anyone’s snoring.

Ace, Devaki, and Walter pitched their tents in the shadow of an alcove. Axel and his dog Enzo were atop a knoll, on a level area with outcrops behind them. Elliot, an immensely talented photographer, chose an elevated spot with a soaring view and organized his kit under the shade of hackberry and maple trees, their branches entwined, his back to an orange cliff. #8266. This South Dakota Hunter Borrowed a Bow and Tagged a 197-Class Deer — His First Archery Buck

Published Nov 8, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It wasn’t the best conditions for bowhunting in central South Dakota on November 3rd. It was misting and drizzling rain and the wind was blowing between 20 and 30 miles per hour.

But Colby Claussen had seen a huge buck the previous week out of a tree stand and decided to buy a ground blind and place it near the trail where the buck had walked.

“I spotted him a week earlier from my stand at nearly 70 yards walking a trail along a field edge near a standing corn field,” Claussen tells Outdoor Life. “He was working scrapes. I decided to buy an enclosed blind and put it in the woods 30 yards off the trail he walked.”

A week later he was in the blind hunting the buck he’d seen on trail cameras off and on for several years.

“I first saw him several years ago through binoculars while hunting,” Claussen says. “The buck was a good 10 pointer then and about 600 yards away – way too far to shoot.”

After that the 20-year-old hunter got trail camera pictures of the buck and watched him grow over several years.

“This year I saw him from my treestand working scrapes, but he was too far for me to try a shot with the bow I’d borrowed from a friend,” says Claussen, a just-graduated student who farms with his family. The giant buck would be his first ever taken with a bow.

By 1 p.m. on Nov. 3, Claussen was in his ground blind, protected from wind and rain. He spotted a couple small bucks and does that afternoon. Just 10 minutes before shooting light ended that day, he spotted the enormous whitetail he was after.

“He stepped out of the woods to work a scrape at 30 yards, but it was too thick to shoot, so I waited,” Claussen says. “The buck stayed on the trail and kept coming toward me until he got in an opening, broadside at 30 yards.”

Claussen drew his bow and shot an arrow tipped with a G5 Megameat 3-blade expandable broadhead. It hit the buck perfectly behind its shoulders, driving through both lungs, clipping its heart, and exiting the massive deer.

“I knew he was hit well, and he went to the treeline, walked in a small circle, and disappeared into the timber,” says Claussen, who owns Sodak Drone Application, an agricultural business. “I went to where he stood and found my arrow and plenty of blood.”

Claussen waited 30 minutes before trailing the deer, then quickly found the buck just 60 yards from where he’d shot it.

He called family members who soon arrived and helped with field dressing and loading the estimated 300-pound buck into a pickup truck. Then they took it to a meat processor, with the buck’s cape and head delivered to a taxidermist.

Read Next: The Best Hunting Blinds of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

A taxidermist measured Claussen’s buck at 198 1/8 inches, and another skilled deer rack scorer came up with 197 7/8 inches. The non-typical rack has nine points on one side, six on the other, with an inside spread of 21.25 inches. Antler base circumferences are 5 3/8 inches. The buck’s estimated age is 5.5 to 6.5 years.

“A couple years ago I had photos of that buck with half a broken rack from fighting,” Claussen says. “I quit hunting him when he broke his rack. But another hunter that year missed him in rifle season.

“I’m sure glad that hunter missed, and I got another chance to take my buck of a lifetime.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8265. How to Judge Trophy Pronghorn in the Field

To judge a trophy pronghorn, evaluate three factors: horn length, prong size, and mass. A 14-inch horn is exceptional, prongs measuring 5 to 6 inches along the upper edge are excellent, and mass is the most critical scoring factor. View the buck from multiple angles and use the animal's own body parts as reference points before you shoot.

Slipping up to the crest of the sage-flecked knoll, we peered down at a pair of stunning tan-and-white pronghorns. “What a buck,” I said, eyeing the closer one. “He’ll go close to 15 inches.”

“Yep,” my guide replied. “Now, if he’ll move a bit, we’ll get a better look at the real trophy behind him.” Making a classic novice’s mistake, I had assumed the taller buck closest to us was superior.

No sight is more emblematic of Western hunting than a pronghorn buck with jet-black horns staring back at you, poised to prance across the prairie at 70 mph. But just how good of a trophy is he? How thick and impressive will those horns be when you wrap your hands around them? Pronghorns are notoriously difficult to judge in the field. So I spoke to three veteran guides who have a century of analyzing antelope horns among them: Bill Ferranti of New Mexico, Bob Daugherty of Colorado, and Pete Dube of Wyoming.

Most hunters focus on this. A 12-inch antelope is average; 13, good; 14, exceptional. Record-book pronghorns often tape 15 to 16 inches. But horns that jut straight up appear longer than they really are, while those curling back and inward, or with ivory tips, ­appear shorter.

The Solution: Try to view the buck from multiple angles so you can add the curl of the horn tips to your length estimate.

Tip: Use the distance between the tip of the animal’s nose and its eye (about 8 inches) or between its ears (12 inches) as a guide to horn length. Also look for a buck whose prongs protrude from the horn an inch or more above its ears.

These are measured from the tip of the prong, along its upper edge, then across to the back center of the horn: 3 to 4 inches is average; 4 to 5, good; 5 to 6, excellent; and 6 to 7, ­record book. What protrudes from the horn is only part of the measurement. You need to figure out how many more inches you gain across the horn to its back axis.

The solution: Judge how much prong actually protrudes from the horn and then add about 2 inches for the width of the horn itself. A prong that extends 3 inches is excellent once you add those couple of inches.

Tip: Use the length of the ear, about 6 inches, for ­comparison. If the full prong measurement is almost that long, it’s a keeper.

This is the most critical factor of all, because it’s measured four times after dividing each horn length into quarters. Good mass tends to make horn length and prongs seem shorter than they really are. Circumference is difficult to judge, even for veteran antelope hunters. Complicating things, some animals have partially flattened bases, making them score lower than antelope with more rounded bases. Basal circumference on outstanding bucks will measure 6 to 7 inches.

The Solution: Study videos and books or visit a taxidermy shop to learn the art of ­judging mass. When you’re hunting, wait until the animal turns sideways to check whether the bases are round or flattened before making a circumference estimate.

Tip: Use an antelope’s eye ­circumference for comparison: It’s about 41â„2 inches. Also look at the diameter of the eye, about 11â„2 inches across. If the antelope’s bases look about an inch wider than the eye width, they’ll likely measure over 7 inches—now that’s a pronghorn.

#8264. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8263. The Best Ski Packs of 2027, Tested in the Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Our 14 testers ran 18 packs through a season of fast transitions, steep bootpacks, and long days to find the best of 2027. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: The best backcountry ski packs of 2027 include the Ortovox Venet 30 ($170) for most skiers, the Raide EX55 ($599) for expeditions, the Dynafit Radical 30 Snow Pack ($190), and the Rab Descendor 40 Ski Pack ($200) for ski mountaineering. Our 14 testers—men and women—evaluated 18 packs over a full season in Colorado, Utah, Alaska, the Alps, and more, judging fit, weight distribution, access, and durability.

When traveling in the backcountry, it’s not just what you bring but how you carry it. Intuitive access points make finding and stashing items easy, and externally fastened gear needs to stay secure without blocking pockets. But making the most of capacity is arguably the most critical feature. As our testers make tracks farther out in the mountains and become more self-reliant, they tend to reach for higher-volume packs that can fit everything they need without overloading them to the point of a skin track gear explosion. We factored comfort into all of it while testing 18 packs, narrowing the field to the best backcountry ski packs of 2027 for every type of ski adventure.

Pros and Cons + Triple-zipper access + Huge hipbelt pocket – A-frame carry blocks pack access and the diagonal carry strap was a little tricky to access

Ski packs work best when you can avoid taking them all the way off and rooting through the main compartment when you need to pull out gear. That means shorter stops in the skin track—if you stop at all—which helps you keep momentum and body temperature up on cold days. The Venet 30 features triple-zipper access to the main compartment, which let our tester quickly grab his water flask while skinning around Hemavan, Sweden, and Helgeland, Norway. The large hipbelt was also a tester favorite. “While I loved the elastic waist on the Ortovox Freerider, the normal hip strap with the pocket on the Venet was a huge plus for general touring,” said one. “On longer days I kept snacks in it and on more freeride days I kept a GoPro, for which easy access allowed me to actually remember to pull my cam out before descents.”

Testers called this the most ergonomic and versatile pack they’ve used from Ortovox, thanks to its simplicity, the comfortable adjustability of its straps, and its full-contact back panel. The mini top pocket was well sized—not too deep and easy to access—and the hidden mini pocket in the avalanche tool compartment was useful for carrying an emergency bivy and small med kit, keeping them “out of the way” of the rest of your gear.

This pack’s ideal use is general touring with the occasional bootpack, but it’s capable as a more technical bag when ropes may be required. It performs well as a freeride sidecountry bag or on longer tours—comfortable for mellow days and functional for technical ones.

Features that would make this pack even more user-friendly: a small zip on the right back side to mirror the bottom zipper for water access, the ability to carry two ice axes (the elastic cord holds only one), and easier access to the pack when using side ski-carry.

Pros and Cons + Modular volume + Rolltop closure – No external helmet carry

Schlepping all your gear on a big hut trip or expedition-style endeavor has long presented a dilemma: how to carry a pack big enough for everything at basecamp while also having a daypack small enough for lighter missions. Bringing two packs is inefficient, but skiing with a few items jiggling loose in a giant frame pack feels cumbersome. The Raide EX55 expands to 75L and carries enormous loads, then cinches down once you’ve emptied most items out, so it skis like a little daypack. “During our big four-day ski traverse out of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, I’d get to the base of a couloir, fill a bivy sack with all our junk, cinch the pack down, and boot up like I had a regular ski pack on,” said our Mammoth-based tester. “It skis incredibly well given how much gear it can swallow.”

Raide accounts for the added weight with thicker shoulder and hip straps and better load lifters than its smaller counterparts, the LF30 and LF40. All of it is ideal for heavier hauls. The EX55 doesn’t just turn into a giant sack and skimp on key features. You can still deploy your probe without taking off your pack—ideal for glacier travel of any kind—and the same goes for the shovel with the pack on one shoulder. Testers called the ski carry systems excellent, and being able to grab an ice tool without removing the pack is invaluable in steep bootpacks. “This pack strips backcountry skiing down to its absolute essentials but lets you do it on a bigger scale,” said one.

The one complaint we heard was that the EX55 lacks the external drop sleeve found in the LF30 and LF40 for carrying helmets and skins, so when the pack is loaded for overnight carries, it’s tough to stuff skins in and out of the front zip pocket. It also makes the pack very tall when fully loaded with a helmet inside.

Weight: 2.31 lbs Size: Women’s, Universal

Pros and Cons + Thick back panel padding + Easy-access diagonal-carry bungee cord strap – Not ideal for those who pack extra gear

When you’re banging out hot laps, your pack should feel like part of your body. This one holds tight to smaller female torsos and disappeared on the back of another Sierra tester last spring as she skied 1,500- to 7,000-foot days on Mount Shasta, in the Eastern Sierra and at Lake Tahoe’s Rubicon Peak. “This pack skied really well, and gear that’s good enough to disappear is my favorite,” she said  after testing other packs with hipbelts that didn’t curve as ergonomically as this one.

Testers appreciated the top, rear-panel, and side zips, which made it easy to organize their stuff inside and keep things like crampons and water readily accessible. The avy gear gets its own pocket with a wide zipper, and an ice axe can be removed without taking the pack off, as can skis with a skimo-style diagonal carry bungee strap.

At 30 liters, it’s right on the edge of fitting everything you might want to carry on a day tour. “When I went out to the Norman Clyde Couloir, conditions were cold and windy, so I wanted to carry more than I usually do for a day tour,” said our tester. “The pack fit snacks, 1 liter of water, a hardshell, a puffy, ski and boot crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a slender rescue sled, avy gear, a small first aid kit, and two pairs of gloves. I was definitely worried about busting the zipper, but it held all day.” The load lifters worked well to support this weight, and the thick back panel kept hard items like water bottles from poking into her back. If you prefer to bring this much stuff or more on most outings, you may find this pack a little too small.

Pros and Cons + Spot-on fit + Long side zipper accesses items of any size – Wobbly elastic diagonal ski carry

Spring ski mountaineering missions can mean longer days, longer approaches, and extra gear—crampons, more water, sometimes ropes—so you need a pack that carries it all in an efficient, functional arrangement. Loading it up is one thing; accessing it is another. The Descendor 40 balances both with a few key features. Our Colorado-based tester was a big fan of the side-access zipper, which is functionally useless if it isn’t long enough. This one is plenty long, and it was the only access point he needed while touring. He could easily pull out anything inside, including a large DSLR camera, skins, and a food bag, and he opened the rolltop closure only during full transitions.

The pack also has the best integration of hydration features. “On the right strap, there is a perfect pocket to carry a soft flask, including a strap to secure the flask against jostling,” our tester said. “I have lost soft flasks while skiing in other packs and am not worried about that on this pack. On the left shoulder strap, there is a small zippered pocket that is an appropriate size to carry items like gels, sunscreen, lip balm, etc. Overall, these features made it easy to stay hydrated and sunscreened on a fast and light ski tour.”

Testers lauded the comfortable back panel, wide hip straps, padded shoulder straps, and load lifters when needed. The pack carries weight well and fits true to size.

This pack is designed for long, efficient ski tours and glaciated summit pushes where ropes and technical gear are needed. It has features for ski mountaineering and carries additional gear like ice tools, with a gear loop for carabiners and a system for quickly strapping skis to the pack. The rolltop is an attempt to make the pack more versatile—a 40L pack that can act as a 25L—but it needs some refinement to better accommodate smaller volumes. Our tester also found the elastic strap for diagonal ski carry too long, and his skis bounced around while bootpacking couloirs.

Built for fast pow laps and and slackcountry days, the Dakine Heli 2.0 is everything you need to stay well equipped on your next mountain adventure. From diagonal ski and splitboard carry to vertical or horizontal snowboard carry, it doesn’t matter your style—it can get your gear wherever you need to go. The pack’s fleece-lined pockets keep your goggles smudge-free, and the snow tool sleeves keep your smaller items organized and accessible. And maybe most importantly, RECCO Technology helps keep you searchable in case of an avalanche or rescue.

Weight: 2.1 lbs (35L, S/M) Sizes: S/M, M/L

Pros and Cons + Easy access to inside storage + Removable snowboard carry straps – Avalanche tool pocket is too large

It’s a bold move to update a classic product, but Black Diamond took a leap on the tried-and-true Cirque by making several big changes. The brand added a side zipper to access the main compartment and more durable materials, including a PFC-free 210D nylon fabric and Dynex grid that’s stronger than the older version and more water repellent. Testers loved these new features and didn’t encounter any durability issues during the whole season of slamming the pack on and off in quick transitions with sharp ski edges and tools rubbing on the outside.

The new Cirque 35 excels on spring missions in the alpine, where quick access to crampons, an ice axe, and other gear is key. “I love a roll-top pack, and this is one feature that I really appreciate,” says one tester who toured it during winter and spring days around Aspen, Colorado. “I was able to throw in an extra layer for tours without hesitation because of the space it offered and how easy it was to get in and out, especially with the large side zipper.” The diagonal ski carry system with a bottom loop and top webbing strap with a hook was quick and easy to deploy in transition, and the ice-axe bungees were a breeze to unfasten on unexpected sections of steep terrain.

Our 6’1″ tester thought the pack was a bit short, and some disliked the hassle of opening both the webbing hook and roll-top buckle to get inside. Snowboard straps are sturdy but removable when you don’t need to carry a board on your pack.

Pros and Cons + Excellent freedom of movement + Compact fit – Limited carrying capacity

Skiing or snowboarding with too much extra space in a backpack allows the contents to rattle around inside, which can be an annoying distraction. Our Montana tester didn’t have that problem when hiking the ridge at Bridger Bowl, their local ski resort, with this compact, 15-liter pack with clever pocket placement and internal organization. Thanks to the low profile, it was comfortable enough to wear on the chairlift, and the fit felt snug while riding, too, with padding in all the right spots on the upper back, hips, and shoulder straps.

“It didn’t flop around at all like bigger packs do when empty, nor did it limit my movement in bumps or when really laying down carves,” another Montana tester said after securing the pack’s wide, sturdy hipbelt. They rode with this pack at Bridger Bowl in sub-freezing temperatures, requiring extra fuel and layers, and didn’t feel that it was too bulky. He also appreciated the glove-friendly A-frame and vertical ski carry options on short sidecountry hikes and bootpacks, along with snowboard straps and an internal avalanche tool compartment for sidecountry missions.

Overall, this is a small, space-efficient pack with smart pockets (fleece-lined goggle and external side zip) for short missions just beyond the gates or for fully-supplied resort laps.

Packs come in various sizes to fit different torso lengths, so measure your spine from the base of your neck to the top of your hips and choose your size accordingly. Torso lengths generally range from 15 inches, or size XS, to 20-plus inches, or size L. Because fit is the single most significant factor in pack comfort and carry, we recommend going to your local gear shop wearing the layers you plan to tour in and trying packs on. The hipbelt should securely wrap your iliac crest, and the back panel shouldn’t hit the back of your head when you’re wearing a helmet.

If half-day backcountry tours are your norm, choose a lower-volume pack, 20 to 30 liters, that fits just the essentials—shovel, probe, water, extra layers, snacks. If you typically spend full days in the backcountry, you’ll want a higher-volume pack, 30 to 40 liters, with room for the extra supplies you’ll need out in the elements. For overnight trips and expeditions, look for a 50-plus-liter pack.

Also make sure your avalanche shovel and probe slip easily in and out of the dedicated avy pouch in an emergency, and that the pack is big enough and organized enough for how you tour. Don’t be afraid to size up if you’re unsure how much space you’ll need—a few extra liters of empty space won’t weigh you down much. If you want to secure your skis to your pack, look for an A-frame or diagonal ski-carry strap system and back-panel suspension that can support the extra weight. The same goes for your helmet: most packs have integrated helmet carry, but not all do, so double-check if it’s essential to you.

Always carry avalanche safety equipment when traveling in the backcountry. That means wearing a beacon and carrying a shovel and probe in your pack. You’ll also need extra layers, a helmet, sufficient hydration—including something hot in an insulated bottle on longer backcountry days—snacks, a first-aid kit, and a basic repair kit.

To nail down the best ski packs of 2027, we seeded 18 products with 14 different testers. Each tester was matched to packs according to their planned objectives, body type, ability level, and testing environments. Then we set testers loose in the mountains, mainly in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Washington, California, and Alaska, with a few trips to Scandinavia and the Alps. Testers jammed gear into packs, stuffed them shut, and pushed them to their limits on both rugged and mellow ski ascents and descents.

We focused on newly designed packs with practical, ski-specific features that make traveling on snow easier, safer, and more enjoyable. We also brought tried-and-true, unchanged models into the mix so you’re seeing the best of what’s available. Comfort is a must, even for packs meant to carry smaller, lighter loads, as is durability, so we asked testers to evaluate straps, back panels, and hipbelt carry alongside the quality of materials.

Every time a pack went out, testers filled out feedback forms assessing fit, weight distribution, ease of access, and even pocket size and placement. Testers noted how easy it was to find what they needed, transition in the skin track, and carry their skis and boards on their backs while climbing steep couloirs. After a full season of rigorous testing, we selected the cream of the crop and reviewed those packs here.

Scott Yorko is a former gear editor for Backpacker, SKI, TransWorld SNOWboarding, and Outside. He lives in Colorado, where he splits his ski time between the world-class resorts around Aspen and the backcountry terrain of the West Elk Mountains. He loves to chase storms and visit pow-shredding friends, many of whom tested this year’s crop of ski packs in places like Alaska, Jackson Hole, the Sierra, Utah, and the Colorado Rockies.

#8262. Are Tree Saddles Really Better Than Treestands for Hunting Whitetails?

Published Nov 8, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Early in my bowhunting career, I set up a ladder stand on top of a ridge that had oaks and plenty of deer sign. On opening morning, I watched a deer parade go down a trail that was 20 yards out of range. I sat in that stand several more times and never had a deer come within bow range. If I had a mobile stand, I could have easily adjusted my hunting strategy to move closer to the active trail.

Mobile hunting for whitetails is all about making aggressive moves and constantly hunting fresh spots. Mobile hunters carry everything they need for a hunt so they can set up on the fresh sign and easily adapt to the conditions. That’s why they need lightweight and easy to use hunting platforms.

That old faithful ladder stand just won’t cut it when you need to slide another 100 yards closer to a bedding area. A mobile setup is also great for public land where you can’t or don’t want to leave your stand. It’s also less expensive than buying multiple permanent stands.

There are three main choices for the mobile hunter: a climber, a hang-on stand, and a tree saddle. I’ve hunted from all three of these platforms in my search for the perfect mobile hunting set up. To help with this comparison, I also reached out to Aaron Warbritton, from The Hunting Public YouTube channel. He’s been at the tip of the spear of the mobile hunting trend and offers a wealth of experience. Together we’ll see how each platform stacks up against each other in five categories: weight, setup, huntability, comfort, and price.

A heavy pack can feel fine for a few minutes, but when yards turn to miles, you feel every pound. For hunting deep in public land, a lightweight set up is a must. Weights will differ depending on the model of stand and climbing method. These weights will give you an idea of what you can expect a complete kit to weigh. Here’s how all three systems compared:

Model: Tethrd Mantis Saddle and Predator platform.

Kit Includes: Saddle, tether, platform, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

Total Weight: 14.1 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

Kit Includes: Stand, safety harness, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

Total Weight: 23.9 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

If weight is your primary concern then a saddle is the clear winner. You can even make the saddle lighter by using a lighter climbing system.

Weight isn’t only a factor when carrying a stand, it also matters for setting it up. This is especially true when hanging a saddle platform or hang-on stand. When you climb to the height you want to hunt, you have to hold the stand or platform in one hand while tightening the stand’s straps with the other. A light platform for a saddle, like the Predator platform (3.3 pounds), is much easier to hang then the heavier base of a hang-on stand (12.2 pounds).

“I would say that now 90 percent of my hunts are with a saddle and a platform; just because it’s lighter, the footprint is smaller, and it’s faster for me to set up,” Warbritton says.

With a saddle and a hang-on, you’ll need your choice of hang-on stand and a climbing method. I use the Lone Wolf Alpha stand and climbing sticks. The stand and sticks were designed to pack neatly together making it a very convenient and easy to use system. You can climb the tree and hang your stand in one trip with practice and some paracord. I’m pretty slow and careful when climbing and it usually takes me 15 to 20 minutes to climb and get set. The hang-on is fast, but the saddle is slightly faster and easier for me to set up.

A climber is attached to the tree before you climb and doesn’t require climbing sticks. There’s also no platform to hang once you reach hunting height. You can scale a tree fairly quickly with one, and it’s a less technical climb than a saddle or platform. However, that speed comes at the cost of versatility. Climbers need a straight, limbless tree, which isn’t always available. I much prefer the versatility of other platforms that allow me to climb almost any tree. If you live in an area that has a lot of trees suitable for a climber, then these negatives might not be such a big deal.

The size of a climber is another negative. “I haven’t hunted out of climbers a ton, but I’ve hunted out of them enough to know I don’t want to use them. Their footprint is so big that when you’re packing them in, the stand gets tangled on stuff,” Warbritton says.

Another reason to move away from climbers is the noise they make when climbing. It’s discouraging to put a lot of effort slipping into your spot, but then make a scraping noise as you ascend into position. This is especially true when hunting close to bedded deer.

By comparison saddles and hang-ons are much stealthier to carry and set up. If you are proficient with either of them, you can be up a tree within earshot of a bedded buck without issue.

Proficiency doesn’t come overnight with any of these platforms, but tree saddles especially take time to learn. The saddle has a steeper learning curve because it’s so different than a traditional treestand. The first time you lean back into your saddle it might feel like leaning back on a rocking chair at the edge of a cliff. However, that uneasy feeling quickly fades and I personally feel much safer in my saddle than I ever felt in a hang-on or climbing treestand. That security comes from the fact that if you fall off your platform it is extremely easy to get back on because the tether is always pulled tight—making the drop almost unnoticeable.

Beyond the saddle’s learning curve, the hang-on and saddle are neck and neck when it comes to packing, setting up, and hunting out of them.

“They’re really close. They definitely have their differences. Whichever one that you decide to use, you need to practice with it. Whether you’re using climbing sticks or strap on steps, you need to practice packing, hanging, and then shooting out of them because they’re different,” Warbritton says.

When the rut kicks in and you basically live in a tree all weekend, a comfortable stand is a must. While all three mobile options are pretty comfortable, the standard treestand seat is hard to beat. Warbritton agrees with that preference.

“The only thing I like about a treestand is if I’m going to sit all day, I’d rather have a treestand,” he says.

Tree saddles are comfortable, but a lot of the comfort in a saddle depends on your tether height because it controls the weight distribution. You’ll need to find a sweet spot that works for you and that takes some practice. I haven’t found that sweet spot for comfort just yet, but I do think that I’ll eventually get the saddle to be as comfortable as my treestands.

Read Next: The Best Tree Stands, Tested and Reviewed

Like weight, the price will depend on the manufacturer and model. Just like our weight evaluation, we’ll compare the products I have personally owned and used.

A Tethrd mantis tree saddle, platform, lineman’s belt, tether, and a set of Lone Wolf climbing sticks will run you around $650. Without climbing sticks the system is about $500. If you want to add some accessories like Ropeman ascenders, pouches, and a recliner, you’ll be looking at spending around $900. It’s not a cheap investment, and you’ll have to decide if the above-stated benefits outweigh the cost.

Hang-ons and climbers are less expensive. A premium climber like the Summit Explorer SD and Hunter Safety System safety harness will run you around $450. A Lone Wolf Alpha hang-on, climbing sticks, Hunter Safety System safety harness, and lineman’s belt will set you back around $500. Again, prices will vary depending on what models, climbing methods, and add on accessories you choose.

Read Next: The Best Tree Saddles of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Warbritton and I both prefer tree saddles because they are lightweight, easy to pack, fast to set up, and make mobile hunting easier. Is it the best system for you? You’ll have to evaluate the features against your hunting needs to make that decision. The good thing is, all three systems will give you the ability to be a mobile hunter.

“I just think that either way you’re going to be hunting mobile and you’re going to have a lightweight setup that’s going to allow you to see more country, learn more stuff, and potentially kill more deer,” Warbritton says.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8261. Des Linden’s Simple (and Somewhat Shocking) 100-Mile Fueling Plan

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Boston Marathon champion Des Linden will toe the line at her first 100-miler on October 31, 2026, at the Javelina Jundred near Fountain Hills, Arizona. To prepare for the distance and hot desert conditions, she worked with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned-ultrarunner-champion Magda Boulet, to dial in her metabolic needs and a fueling plan. She will primarily rely on liquid calories, with the addition of some more out-of-the-box products like “cooling” menthol gels, while understanding that mid-race adjustments will be key.

For Boston Marathon champion-turned-competitive ultrarunner Des Linden, one question keeps driving her forward: “Can I do this?”

After years of racing some of the world’s most prestigious road marathons, the two-time Olympian is shifting her focus to off-road competitions. On October 31, she’ll attempt her most ambitious athletic endeavor yet when she toes the start line of the Javelina Jundred, a 100-mile trail race through Arizona’s Sonoran Desert that also serves as a Golden Ticket race into the 2027 Western States 100.

“I feel like part of me is just missing being afraid of something; the unknown,” Linden tells Trail Runner. “What is this going to pull out of me? What is this going to ask of me? That’s all really fascinating.”

In addition to the distance—nearly 40 miles more than Linden has ever covered in one go–Javelina presents a slew of unfamiliar challenges. One of the biggest is fueling and hydration over the course of 13-plus hours in desert conditions. Linden got a small taste, literally, at the Black Canyon 50K in February. It was her first ultramarathon and she acknowledged after the race that all of those years of fueling on the roads was only so helpful.

“I went into Black Canyon 50k with a loose fueling plan—to have a Gu at each aid station and sip on an electrolyte beverage between stations,” Linden said. “I wasn’t diligent about it during the race and certainly didn’t account for the time required for trail miles versus road miles. After the race, I realized it was a very easy place to make improvements, and getting it dialed before MDS would be important.”

It’s a relatable learning curve that Linden has taken seriously in the eight months since. Together with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned ultrarunning-champion Magda Boulet, Linden has tested her metabolic needs under hot ultramarathon conditions to develop a (somewhat surprising) fueling plan for October 31.

Linden retired from professional road running in 2025 after an illustrious career that included two Olympic Games, two runner-up finishes at both the Chicago and Boston Marathons, and an iconic win at the 2018 Boston Marathon—becoming the first American woman to do so in 33 years. Rather than hanging up her running shoes, Linden is targeting some of the world’s most prestigious trail races.

“I think a lot of this part of my career is getting away from comparing myself to my former self. So this is uncharted territory for me,” Linden says.

This past April, Linden, 43, competed in only her second ultra-trail event, finishing third at Marathon des Sables (MDS), a six-day stage race in the southern Moroccan Sahara often referred to as the “Toughest Footrace on Earth.” While Linden has spent her career refining how she fuels for peak performance and recovery, her MDS experience reinforced just how critical nutrition is to sustaining her endurance and rebounding after hours on her feet. She adds that ultrarunning has pushed her to reevaluate her approach to nutrition as she continues to take on longer and more demanding challenges.

“The distance itself makes nutrition so much more important,” Linden says. “You can’t cover that distance if you’re skimping or shortcutting getting the calories in throughout the day.”

The Javelina Jundred is an open and exposed course. The race is defined by heat: the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit and the average low is roughly 58 degrees. Managing more time on her feet also creates more opportunities for things to go awry. Research has long suggested that heat stress can reduce appetite: A 2018 study in Nature found that exercise suppresses appetite by heating up a region of the brain responsible for regulating eating. Of course, this appetite suppression is counterproductive since you are expending lots of extra energy while running, and create a negative feedback loop that self-perpetuates.

Along with dehydration, racing in the heat creates a unique set of challenges. Linden has been working hard to prepare for them.

To prepare for the challenge, Linden enlisted experts from Gu Energy Labs, based in Berkeley, California, including Roxanne Vogel, Ph.D., nutrition scientist, exercise physiologist, and director of research and education, and Magda Boulet, Gu Energy Labs president and one of the world’s most accomplished ultrarunners. Boulet’s own evolution from Olympic marathoner to Western States 100, Leadville 100, and Marathon des Sables champion has made her a valuable resource for Linden’s own ultramarathon journey.

“I imagine most ultrarunners will look and be like ‘you’re not ready at all.’ But they don’t necessarily know that behind the scenes I have the ultrarunner,” Linden says.

Ahead of MDS this spring, Linden underwent laboratory testing at Gu’s Performance Lab with the goal of understanding her energy expenditure, hydration needs, and fueling tolerance during ultramarathon efforts. As part of the assessment, Vogel set out to measure Linden’s sweat rate and sodium losses under heat stress, her caloric demands at race pace, and how her body uses carbohydrate versus fat in simulated desert conditions.

The data helped Vogel develop an individualized metabolic and hydration profile for Linden. Vogel discovered that Linden isn’t a very salty sweater, and she also learned that Linden needs approximately 10 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight per day. (For a 120-pound person, that’s roughly 550 grams of carbs.)

Going into MDS, the team developed a precise nutrition strategy for Linden, which included Gu Roctane Drink Mix along with gels and chews for her on-course fueling. After each stage, Linden leaned on nut butter and Roctane Protein Recovery Drink Mix to supply the necessary carbohydrates, electrolytes, and 20 grams of whey protein. Her dinner included a savory dehydrated potato mash with added protein and sodium. Linden also integrated Gu Roctane BCAA capsules before and after the stages to support muscle repair and reduce soreness.

Vogel says those core principles will be part of Linden’s approach at Javelina, but the demands of a single day 100-mile race in the Arizona desert will require some adjustments. For Javelina, liquid calories will be the backbone of her nutrition strategy. The target is to consume approximately 16 ounces (500 milliliters) of Roctane Drink Mix per hour. Per 16-ounce serving, it offers 250 calories, 60 grams of carbs, and 320 milligrams of sodium. Linden also plans to integrate some products that remain under development, Vogel says, including Roctane MC-318, a patented menthol-based energy gel designed to help athletes feel perceptually cooler. The product is not yet commercially available, but has already been tested by athletes at races such as Badwater 135, Western States 100, and Marathon des Sables.

The Javelina course consists of five loops along rolling desert singletrack. It’s a format that allows for both Linden and her crew to accurately anticipate her arrival at aid stations, where she’ll be able to replenish supplies and, crucially, will allow for crew to frequently assess how she’s managing the nutrition and hydration plan.

The terrain will help determine when Linden takes in different forms of fuel. Uphill sections, when she’s moving more slowly, provide an opportunity to take gels or chews. On downhills, when she wants to let her legs unwind and rip down as fast as possible, she’ll focus more on liquids. Her approach also reflects a shift from road marathon racing, where fueling opportunities are often more structured and brief.

“In the marathon, [every] 5K you grab the bottle, you want eight to 10 ounces and you want to get rid of the bottle as quickly as possible. We have the luxury of carrying it and sipping on it, and also strategizing,” Linden says.

Temperature will be one of the most significant variables. Research has found that during prolonged exercise in the heat, gastrointestinal symptoms are greater.

“People think it has to be really hot for them to need to make changes to their nutrition or their electrolyte plan,” Vogel says. “The cutoff is somewhere around 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Above that, you’re certainly going to be at an increased level of needs in terms of your hydration and electrolytes, plus also potentially your carbohydrate needs. Even in somewhat moderately warm temperatures, athletes can be needing more than what they would normally take in.”

As the temperature rises throughout the day over the course of the race, Linden anticipates leaning more heavily on liquids. The drink mix can provide fluid and carbohydrates while helping her meet her electrolyte needs, and gels with water will fill any gaps.

“She’s never done a [single day] race this long. The longer you’re out there, the more likely your gut is going to have some issues,” Vogel says. “When you’re exercising, blood flow is going to your working muscles. Less of it is going to your digestive track. So that’s one thing that’s putting stress on the system that makes it harder to digest and absorb [nutrition]. Hence the whole reason for things like gels. They’re easy to digest.”

During the hottest part of the day, Vogel says the team may decrease Linden’s carbohydrate intake to account for changes in digestive tolerance. But as temperatures fall into the night, they’ll look to increase her carbs. Vogel says caffeine will require similar consideration.

“During very hot weather events, caffeine can actually be triggering to the gut in a bad way,” Vogel says. “Rather than following a fixed schedule regardless of conditions, we might actually pull back on caffeine during the heat of the day and start to strategically add it back in as it cools off later in the day.”

Another factor to consider: flavor fatigue, when sensory receptors on your tongue that detect flavor become less responsive with repeated consumption.

“Flavor fatigue is something we know and understand. In hot environments, you don’t generally want to have things that are what we call indulgent—chocolates and caramels and vanillas that are going to stay heavy on the palate. We want more things like citrus and light fruity or even sour, tart flavors that are going to clear the palate or stimulate some thirst,” Vogel says.

Ultimately, the goal is to make the strategy simple to execute, Vogel says. Linden’s success will depend not only on having a precise nutrition plan, but on adjusting on the fly when fatigue and discomfort begin to accumulate.

“I feel like it’s a race within itself. Did I try to execute as well as possible? Did I follow the plan? Did I make good decisions?” Linden says. “I want to finish, and I think there’s so many things that can go in so many different directions in that amount of time and that distance. So if I fueled enough to get myself through 100 miles, that’s a victory.”

#8260. Black Friday Generator Deals Are Starting Early—Up to 44% Off

Whether you’re weathering a power outage or camping off-grid in an RV, a generator is one of the most useful and tools you have at your disposal. While these units are worth their weight in gold when you really need them, but they tend to get pricey.
