#8259. Hunters Can’t Really Improve Wild Whitetail Genetics. Here’s Why

Published Nov 8, 2026 4:52 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was the year we’d been waiting for at the family deer camp. All summer and fall we pulled trail camera photos of more—and bigger—bucks than had ever been seen on the property. It was a far cry from the early 90s, when the bucks my dad and uncles did spot tended to have a signature narrow spread with tall, skinny tines. Now, nearly 30 years later, we’re finally seeing a caliber of deer we weren’t even sure the property was capable of supporting. It’s taken a lot of intensive habitat improvement and discipline, but it’s working.

Still, there was probably a faster way to get here. It should have taken years, not decades, to improve our whitetail habitat. And there are still things we’re trying to figure out—like how to kill those bucks now that we’ve got them. So, I decided to find out what a lot of whitetail hunters get wrong by talking to some hunters who have been succeeding at the management game for a long time.

Typically, a cull buck is one that deer managers have identified as genetically inferior and should be removed from the wild herd. This might be a deer whose antlers are too small or too funky to keep in the gene pool. Studies show that killing these deer solely on the basis of selective harvest (rather than for the traditional reasons of fun, meat, etc.) is ultimately a waste of a good buck tag.

“Many hunters simply believe that you can influence antler quality through genetics in the wild,” says Kip Adams, chief conservation officer of the National Deer Association (formerly QDMA). “We know very clearly that yes, behind a fence—when you can pick which buck is doing the breeding and which doe is doing the breeding—[you] absolutely can influence the genetics. In the wild, it’s very clear we cannot do that.”

This is for a few reasons. For one, does are contributing half the antler DNA to buck fawns. (If you can identify which does have favorable antler genes from your treestand, please share with the rest of the class.) Also, the rut doesn’t lead to quite as many fawns as you might think.

“It’s not like the biggest buck out there dominates all the does and sires the most fawns,” Adams says, noting that the average U.S. fawn recruitment right now is .59, or less than one fawn per doe. “Research shows that most bucks sire very few fawns during the course of their life. We can’t dominate the gene pool that way.”

“We can’t predict what a buck’s son will have—from an antler standpoint—by looking at a buck’s antlers,” says Adams.

Let’s say that again for the hunters in the back: Just because a buck has big antlers doesn’t mean his offspring will. And just because a buck has small antlers doesn’t mean his offspring will have small antlers. (Part of that goes back to the fact that you can’t tell what kind of antler genes a doe is carrying around.)

That all boils down to Adams’ original point: A hunter cannot influence the genetics of a wild deer herd. Selective buck culling to optimize antler size doesn’t work. So, what can hunters do, if they want to shoot bigger bucks? It’s a simple two-part plan rooted in the classic QDM refrain. First, let deer get older.

“We tend to see and hear about more bigger bucks than ever before because older deer are encompassing a higher percentage of the total buck harvest today than ever before,” Adams says. “Hunters today are letting deer get older at unprecedented levels, and that’s the reason that, across the whitetails’ range, we see, hear of, photograph, and shoot bigger deer than ever before.”

The 2021 Deer Report reveals that during the 2019-20 deer season, 39 percent of all antlered bucks harvested were at least 3.5 years old. That’s the highest national average ever recorded.

The second thing you can do if you want to increase antler size? Increase the available nutrition for deer. This means increasing habitat quality, decreasing the number of deer using the habitat (that is, shooting more does), or both.

It’s all good and well to recommend passing bucks to let them mature, but what does that look like on the ground? Some of the most successful big deer hunters follow this advice, and with good results.

Brothers Brent and Justin Cearlock, two of the Illinois hunters behind the world-record whitetail, enjoy considerable success year after year. Part of this is because of where they live, in the prime big-buck county of eastern Illinois. But it’s also because they pass more bucks than they shoot, even with two buck tags apiece per season.

Read Next: Two Years After the World-Record Buck, the Cearlock Brothers Are Still on a Roll

“I have no intention of shooting a deer younger than five, unless it has just a substantially huge rack,” says Justin, who mostly relies on trail camera history to help him establish age estimates. “I don’t care if I think the deer is four. I’m just going to let him get to five, just to see what happens.”

This past season, Brent made the call on a stud buck that didn’t meet this age threshold. Instead of picking up his bow that morning, he grabbed his phone and shot some video.

“I passed a phenomenal deer—the biggest buck I’ve ever let walk in my life,” Brent says. “He was already in the mid-160s, flirting with the 170-inch mark as a 4-year-old deer. I called him Will, because I didn’t know if I would have the willpower to pass him.”

The guys could only imagine what Will might look like in fall 2021. Brent ended up killing a lower-scoring buck that same day: a deer that was at least seven years old, and that he had history with.

“We’re very fortunate to have access to the properties we do. If you don’t have good properties, you’re not going to shoot big deer,” Brent says. “But we do put a lot of effort into it and we pass deer that most people probably wouldn’t pass. There are a lot of guys that say they’ll pass a deer like that. But when they’re standing there and it’s getting dark, they’re like, I’m shooting that deer.”

Brent didn’t regret his decision—the older buck meant a lot to him—but he couldn’t help feeling torn when he learned a neighbor shot Will a few weeks later.

“Passing a big one comes with risk, and I am genuinely happy for the other hunter to get a great buck like that,” Brent says. “But I’d be lying if I said part of me isn’t sincerely disappointed that we just lost what we thought might be our No. 1 target buck next year.”

Often the decision to pass a deer is fraught because of the property itself. Other hunters with permission and neighboring hunters are just two of the many factors that reduce a deer’s odds of surviving into the next season. And the Cearlocks don’t begrudge anyone who wants to shoot younger bucks: They’ve been those guys themselves, earlier in their hunting careers. But the knowledge that a neighbor might shoot a buck isn’t enough to make them abandon their management strategy in the heat of the moment.

“There’s a lot of things that can happen,” Brent acknowledges. “But if you shoot them, they’re definitely not going to make it to five.”

This past deer season, Rick Dahl secured access to a new whitetail property in central Missouri. Dahl believes the new farm, which is in the same county as the parcels he currently hunts, actually holds better potential for bigger bucks. The new property is promising for a few reasons, including its superior soil quality, fewer neighbors to compete with, and the anecdotal evidence that big bucks are being harvested nearby. The fact that the new property doesn’t have any shooter bucks on it yet doesn’t seem to faze him.

“The food supply is very limited on the new farm,” Dahl says, who is a lifelong Missouri deer hunter and chairman of the NDA board. “[But] it’s in the right area and, if we give the deer there what they need to eat, time will tell whether we’ll be able to produce a bigger-antlered deer there.”

Although the property has fertile soil, Dahl says the food supply is limited because it hasn’t been managed for deer yet. A mature forest canopy has prevented understory growth, and many of the tillable fields were used as cattle pasture. Dahl’s no biologist, but he still knows good soil is important for growing big deer.

Dahl conducted a trail camera survey late last year, which revealed a relatively even age-class distribution of deer—and some clues to support his hunch that nutrition is currently a limiting factor for antler growth. The photos of yearling bucks seem to be mostly spikes, instead of fork-horns. And, with the exception of one deer with an extra point, not a single buck on the property seemed to have more than eight points.

“That was really interesting to me,” Dahl says, who noticed four bucks in the 4- and 5-year-old age class that probably scored 140 inches. “It takes a big 8-pointer to score like that. So, there’s clearly an 8-point genetic thing going on there. I will be really interested to see what transpires over the next three to five years as we begin to introduce more food.”

Read Next: 9 Ways to Score Permission on Private Property

What confused me about this particular endeavor—investing time and money in a whole new property that’s going to need careful timber, habitat, and food plot management—is that Dahl currently has a 4.5-year-old minimum age limit agreement with his hunting buddies on the excellent properties they’ve already got. Why not just raise the age limit for shooter bucks to five, like the Cearlock brothers?

“I’m at the point where I think five and a half is the right age [for me],” Dahl says. “But I also realize that everybody’s at a different stage in the maturation process that we all go through as hunters. My hunting partner is a perfect example. He hasn’t shot a lot of bucks. And if we say we’re not going to shoot anything less than five years old, well, what are we doing? We just went from five deer out there we can hunt to two. At some point you’ve restricted yourself. And for me, if there’s only one deer on the farm that I’m willing to shoot, then the question becomes, ‘Is it really fun anymore?’ And maybe that deer jumps the fence and gets shot by the neighbor on October 30. What do you do? Are you just done?”

Happily for Dahl, he doesn’t have to pick. He can tinker with the new farm, and see if those nutritional improvements eventually support the 4.5-year-old bucks he’s interested in.

The Northeast isn’t exactly known for dedicated deer management. This is a combination of multiple factors, including high hunter numbers in states like Pennsylvania and poorer soil quality. But Neil Dougherty, the president of NorthCountry Whitetails consulting services, finds the challenges of creating QDM programs for clients that much more rewarding.

“Iowa is like Disneyland—it’s fake,” Dougherty laughs. “It’s such a wonderful place in those areas where deer have the ability to explode like that, but it’s not the everyman’s hunt. It’s such a foreign thing to most people who are trying to play this deer game.”

When Dougherty examines a deer property, he takes into account 17 different factors—from native habitat to huntability—to determine the property’s potential. He can almost always improve a property to help “unlock the genetic potential” of the deer that are there. But he’s not a magician, either.

“There’s a magic intersection with the amount of food that’s produced on a property, and the amount of deer that are there to consume that food,” Dougherty says, “The problem is, in some big woods country, that could be eight deer per square mile. That kind of hunting sucks.”

While almost all the properties Dougherty works on need some serious rehabilitation of the natural habitat, the biggest problem with a new property usually lies not with the land, but the client.

“When I show up, there’s almost always a hunting strategy that’s flawed,” Dougherty says. “Just about every property has a hunting strategy that does not lend itself to the intersection of the hunter coming in contact with 5-year-old deer. [Those hunters] just haven’t been exposed to 5-year-old deer. They don’t understand what it takes to speak the same language.”

If you broke down those flaws, Dougherty estimates poor understanding of the wind is to blame about 40 percent of the time. That’s a big improvement compared to even 10 years ago. Today’s hunters are generally much more sophisticated at hunting downwind, he says, and being aware of steady or swirling wind patterns.

“Access is the biggest issue I’m finding. It’s super hard to get out of these spots—getting in isn’t that hard to do, but getting out in the dark and not blowing up the area? That requires a lot of discipline. And sometimes we’re limited by the physical characteristics of a property.”

While Dougherty is a habitat expert, his consulting work involves much more than recommending where to put food plots and what to plant in them. At the end of the day, he’s teaching clients how to hunt.

“I would encourage people to not get caught up in this whole genetic thing,” Dougherty advises. “Learn what your [deer] potential is on the property you hunt, know what you’re doing when it comes to habitat, and just be happy with what you’re doing.”

So, even if the stars align and you end up with big deer consistently using your property, the question remains: Can you kill one of them?

As it turns out, I couldn’t last fall. When I did finally get the biggest buck on the place in front of me, I choked. Painful lesson though it was, it was a reminder that managing for mature deer isn’t like shooting fish in a barrel. Sure, it can be a lot easier when you’ve got 5,000 acres and no neighbors or public land for miles around. But that’s unrealistic for most hunters. Even some basic habitat work and personal discipline can improve the number and quality of deer where you hunt.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8258. ‘Not Your Daddy’s 22.’ This Is The Best 22 Creedmoor Ammo for Deer Hunting

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

New cartridges like the 22 Creedmoor and 22 ARC have been developed alongside the modern practice of leveraging heavy-for-caliber bullets into better downrange performance and, as it turns out, the 22 Creedmoor is a stone-cold deer killer. There are still relatively limited factory ammo options compared to legacy cartridges, and if you’re looking for the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer specifically, there are a couple of important considerations. Here’s a look at five of the solid options we have tested for accuracy and velocity, using the bullets that have killed deer and other big game with. Being that Hornady brought the cartridge to SAAMI for standardization, they have the widest variety of factory ammo, but there are other good options too.

People get a lot of big feelings when you broach the subject of shooting big-game animals with .22-caliber rifles, so it’s important to talk about what we mean, and what we don’t. There have undoubtedly been thousands of deer killed with various varmint bullets and .22 rimfire cartridges with a wide variety of results.

That’s not what we’re talking about here.

As numerous insightful old timers discovered by loading cartridges like the .220 Swift, .22/250 Remington, and .223 Remington with more purposeful bullets — sometimes requiring tighter twist barrels — .22-caliber centerfires kill deer very effectively.

The 22 Creedmoor, with the same bullets and barrel length, will leave even the great Swift in the dust, and it’s specifically designed to work best with modern, long, high-BC bullets that maintain their speed and terminal effectiveness hundreds of yards beyond what traditional 40- to 60-grain .224 bullets could. These bullets are perfectly capable of delivering decisive penetration and trauma on any reasonable shot at a deer.

There are a couple important things to consider when picking the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer. First is bullet weight and construction. There isn’t currently a plethora of 22 Creed factory ammo on the market, but it’s wise to avoid the varmint-specific loads. Many varmint bullets are designed specifically to be fragile. At some of the velocities you’ll see from these 22 Creed varmint loads, the volatile bullets can sometimes not penetrate well.

An example of this is Hornady’s 62-grain ELD-VT, launched with the 22 ARC in mind. According to Hornady their shooters, after killing hundreds of coyotes, noticed that they saw a higher percentage of them running after being hit when the 62-grain ELD-VT was used in the 22 CM than when it was launched slightly slower out of the ARC. The problem was remedied with a slightly heavier 69-grain slug. Deer aren’t exceptionally big or dense animals, and there are other ammo options that will work well.

The other consideration isn’t as straightforward, and is one significant drawback of the 22 Creedmoor. Its standardized twist rate of 1:8 accommodates those more fragile bullets at high velocities while generally stabilizing the heavy-for-caliber 80-plus-grain bullets — but not always. At low elevations and in cold weather, your bullets can lose stability, and your accuracy can go to hell completely.

I first noticed this while shooting at about 28 degrees Fahrenheit and 1,000 feet of elevation. This barrel consistently printed 20-shot samples under an inch with the 80-grain ELD-X, but, beyond 600 yards, my bullets were dropping way more than they had been doing a few days prior when it was warmer. Later, at 0 degrees Fahrenheit, groups at 100 yards opened up to nearly 6 inches with the same bullets. I’ve documented this instability, which varies from barrel to barrel, in several guns now.

The takeaway is that if you are going to be hunting late season at low elevation in cold temperatures, either choose a bullet that will work reliably in a 1:8-twist barrel, or at least test your rifle and ammo in those conditions before hunting.

The 80-grain ELD-X is one of the best all-around .22-cal performers for larger game. This bullet follows the same general design as other ELD-X bullets, featuring a lead core and mechanical internal locking ring to control expansion. It has Hornady’s heat shield tip with DRVT for more consistent drag. This is one of the most efficient hunting-specific .22-cal bullets there is, with a BC that allows it to stay above 2,000 fps for over 600 yards in the 22 Creedmoor. The most unique characteristic to this bullet — compared to the ELD-X in other calibers — is that it has a proportionally thicker jacket. This was to ensure controlled expansion even at velocities over 3,000 fps.

This bullet has proven to penetrate well and do a lot of damage. I shot a whitetail buck with the 80-grain ELD-X loaded in a .223, which would have been the equivalent of about a 450-yard shot from the 22 Creed. It hit the buck, which was quartering to, through the front shoulder and exited halfway back the ribs on the opposite side. I’ve also executed a similar shot on a huge black bear from about 15 yards with a 22 ARC — leaving the bullet under the offside hide after about 18 inches of penetration.

This is an all-around performer in the 22 Creedmoor, but is more optimal in a 1:7-twist barrel. If you’re planning on using it in cold weather, you should test it beforehand.

Many hunters will intentionally steer clear of match ammunition and Hornady does not recommend this ammo for deer hunting. Sometimes folks try stuff without asking permission, however, and it ends up working pretty damned well. Now, seeing how well the 80-grain ELD-X works, I’m not compelled to choose the nearly identical ELD-M bullet over it. They have the same BC and often have nearly the same point of impact and velocity. But this load has crushed a lot of bucks and is a favorite of Derrick Ratliff of Horizon Firearms and one of the big players in bringing the 22 Creed to the commercial market.

The ELD-M bullet will generally be more fragile than the ELD-X, and it creates even more violent wound cavities. This doesn’t mean it explodes on shoulders and won’t penetrate — that’s not the case. But when seeing the holes it puts through deer, you may want to tone it down. There’s no harm if you choose a more rigidly constructed bullet, and you should always be thoughtful about the shots you do take by keeping your bullet construction in mind. Still, this ammo is out there killing bucks with authority.

If you need or want a monolithic copper bullet, this will likely be the only factory option you can find. It uses a 65-grain CX bullet, which is a comfortable 1:8-twist bullet. In testing, Hornady found the 70-grain CX — made for the 1:7-twist 22 ARC — doesn’t stabilize well. I was able to shoot a pronghorn with this bullet, handloaded for an 18-inch 22 Creedmoor, before factory ammo was available. The bullet passed through both shoulders and the buck was dead before he hit the ground.

If you’re a fan of shoulder-shooting deer, this is a bullet you will be very happy with. The CX is designed for high weight retention and won’t produce a wound as violent as the ELD-X or ELD-M, but it is a penetrating son-of-a-gun. The 65-grain CX has a lower BC than the 80-grain lead-core bullets, but has enough velocity to help it maintain a similar effective range. For most deer hunters choosing a 22 Creed, you’ll be hunting at distances where that lower BC won’t come into play.

We’ve been big fans of the Federal Fusion line for deer ammo because it’s affordable, shoots well, and delivers great terminal performance. Federal just announced this 22 Creedmoor deer ammo, but I saw the press release a few days after buying some in a local store, so it should be available for rifle seasons. This is probably the most affordable 22 Creed ammo that’s deer-appropriate, and it features the same plated jacket as other Fusion bullets.

I’ve gone through a couple boxes of this and the ammo shot pretty well. It averaged 3,100 fps from a 22-inch barrel, which would put it around 125 fps slower than box velocity of 3,300 fps in a 24-inch barrel. Velocities can vary depending on several factors, but it does track with a lot of factory 22 CM ammo in the 70-80-grain range which ranges from 3,050 to 3,200 fps from 20-inch barrels — the most common contemporary barrel length.

If maximizing efficiency is important to you, there are better bullets, but this should work comfortably at any temperature in a standard 1:8 twist barrel, and will deliver great performance for the needs of most deer hunters.

Another excellent option for deer would be Nosler’s 70-grain AccuBond offering. This is more of a legacy bullet — made for 1:9- or 1:8-twist barrels — that’s also loaded in .223, rather than one of the more optimized 22 Creedmoor options. I would love to see Nosler come out with a heavier, more efficient option that leverages the Creed’s case and chamber design and load this to a bit more competitive speeds. Still, this is a deadly and effective bullet at normal deer-hunting distances, and would be a good choice.

Modern bullets are what really make the 22 Creedmoor shine as a deer cartridge. We have options that are more efficient with more predictable performance than ever. If you want to hunt deer with a 22 Creedmoor, pick ammo that will fit how and where you hunt.

Read Next: Best Ammo for Deer Hunting, Tested for Accuracy

Most people won’t have to worry about bullet stability with factory ammo, but it’s something you need to pay attention to at low elevation in temperatures below freezing. As with any hunting rifle and ammo, the most important factor is you. Pick a rifle and ammo you like and get out there and practice.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8256. Vail Has Free On-Mountain Grills— Here’s Where to Find Them

Skiing isn’t exactly a budget-friendly sport. Between lift tickets, equipment rentals, and overpriced on-mountain meals, the costs can add up quickly. But tucked away at one of Colorado’s most famous ski resorts is an unexpected way to save money on lunch. Instead of spending a small fortune at an on-mountain restaurant, skiers can bring their own meats and grill them slopeside.

My husband and I have done exactly that; we packed our own meat for a midday cookout between runs at Vail Ski Resort. It’s one of those experiences that feels almost too good to be true, especially at a resort where even a casual lunch comes with a price.

And while saving money is certainly part of the appeal, there’s something special about taking a break from skiing to grill your own lunch surrounded by the Rocky Mountains.

Located in Blue Sky Basin, Belle’s Camp offers a different kind of dining experience. Rather than ordering from a menu, guests can bring their own food and use the public grills to prepare lunch.

“Belle’s Camp is meant to be a different kind of on-mountain dining experience,” says Kevin Delonay, Vail Mountain’s senior director of food and beverage. “Guests bring their own food, gather with friends and family, and make lunch part of their day in Blue Sky Basin.”

It’s a surprisingly simple concept. Pack whatever you’d like to eat, carry it with you while skiing, and head to Belle’s Camp when you’re ready for lunch. Burgers, hot dogs, and steaks are all possibilities, although you’ll want to consider how easily your food can be transported in a backpack.

Visitors should also pack whatever they need to enjoy their meal, including any necessary utensils, condiments, and other supplies. Since you’re carrying everything onto the mountain, keeping things simple can make the experience much easier.

The grills are available during Belle’s Camp operating hours when Blue Sky Basin is open, although availability is subject to mountain operations and weather conditions.

“There are plenty of places at Vail where we cook the meal for you,” Delonay says. “Belle’s is special because we provide the setting and guests create the experience themselves.”

One of the biggest advantages of grilling your own lunch is the potential savings, especially for families or groups skiing together.

At Vail, a typical on-mountain cafeteria lunch can cost around $20 per person, while a more upscale dining experience can cost considerably more. At The 10th, Vail’s full-service restaurant at the top of Gondola One, a Wagyu cheeseburger is listed at $45. For a family of four, a lunch on the mountain could add up to $80 to $180 before drinks or other extras.

Keep reading: Everything You Need To Know About The Hottest New Ski Lunch Trend

Instead, visitors can stop at a grocery store before their ski day and stock up on ingredients for a fraction of the cost. For example, a pack of hot dogs, buns, and a few toppings could feed several people for around $15 to $20. Burgers are another relatively inexpensive option, while those looking to make lunch more of an occasion can bring steaks.

Of course, the exact savings depend on what you purchase and how many people are in your group. But for families or friends already spending hundreds of dollars on lift tickets, rentals, and other ski expenses, packing lunch is one of the easiest ways to cut costs.

And unlike eating a cold sandwich on a chairlift, grilling your own meal gives you a chance to sit down, relax, and enjoy a warm meal on the mountain with a new sense of appreciation.

Despite being one of the resort’s more unusual experiences, Belle’s Camp isn’t necessarily something every first-time visitor knows about.

According to Delonay, much of its popularity has developed organically, with skiers introducing their friends and family to the experience.

“Belle’s Camp has really grown through word of mouth, and I think that’s part of its charm,” he says. “People discover it, bring their friends back and start their own traditions.”

That’s part of what makes the experience so memorable. Some visitors might stop for a quick burger between runs, while others turn lunch into a full-blown gathering with friends.

“We see everything from a simple lunch with friends to groups that really turn it into an occasion,” Delonay says. “That creativity is part of what makes Belle’s so much fun.”

For my husband and me, grilling lunch at Belle’s Camp was a fun change from the typical ski resort dining experience. It’s not every day you get to cook your own meal in the middle of one of the country’s most famous ski resorts.

If you love grilling your own lunch on the mountain, Vail isn’t your only option in Colorado.

Loveland Ski Area, near the Continental Divide, also lets skiers bring their own food and cook lunch without visiting a traditional restaurant.

The resort has four on-mountain cabins that the public can use for free, each equipped with propane grills. Visitors are welcome and encouraged to pack their own food and prepare a meal during their ski day.

It’s a particularly appealing option for families and groups who want a warm lunch without paying on-mountain restaurant prices. But beyond the savings, it’s also a fun way to slow down and enjoy a different side of skiing.

After all, some of the most memorable moments on the mountain don’t happen on the slopes. Sometimes, they’re as simple as grilling lunch with friends and family between runs.

#8255. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

In running and in life: Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts celebrate with their wives as well as crews after setting the world record.

#8253. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Got your own tale of getting benighted? Submit it here.

#8252. Lindsey Vonn Is Headed for Her 9th Surgery. She’s Still Thinking About Skiing.

Lndsey Vonn inspects the slope before the second official training for the women's downhill event at the Tofane Alpine Skiing Centre during Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games (Photo: Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images)

Lindsey Vonn is just days away from her ninth surgery in as many months, and the three-time Olympic medalist is still thinking about skiing.

On November 9, Vonn, 42, is heading into what’s slated to be the final surgery on her left leg following her severe crash during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in February. In an exclusive interview with Forbes, the alpine skier detailed her upcoming surgery.

“The plan is to remove all of the hardware, finally fix the ACL, and hopefully that’s my last surgery,” she told Forbes.

In February 2026, Vonn started the Olympic downhill race despite rupturing the ACL in her left knee just days earlier. After taking an aggressive line through the first few turns, Vonn clipped a gate just 13.4 seconds into her run, pushing her off course at the Tofane Alpine Skiing area.

The impact sent her spinning through the air before she crashed onto the icy surface, ending her race. Vonn was eventually airlifted to a hospital and diagnosed with complex fractures of the two bones in her lower left leg. Doctors put three plates and up to 20 screws in her leg, but couldn’t fix her ACL until her bones healed properly, she told Parade.

In the weeks following her initial surgery, Vonn shared that her injuries were so severe that she had to undergo an emergency fasciotomy, a procedure used to treat acute compartment syndrome. This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when pressure builds up around muscle groups, restricting blood flow or damaging muscles, tendons, and fascia. Colorado-based surgeon Dr. Tomas Hackett performed the complicated operation that saved her left leg from being amputated.

In a video shared to Instagram, the ski champion is sailing on a hydrofoil, writing that the event “was a big step in my recovery that made me incredibly happy. It may not have been snow but … it was one step closer to skiing.”

“I know I won’t be doing this, or much else, for quite some time after this next surgery, but I know I’ll get back to it,” she continued. “Eventually, I will.”

She said she expects to be on crutches for about four weeks and still has at least six months of rehabilitation in the works.

In 2010, Vonn became the first American woman to win Olympic gold in downhill skiing. Wherever she winds up, whether it’s slopeside or downhill, Vonn will always be our favorite comeback story.

#8251. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8249. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.

#8245. A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

#8244. The Best Ski Gear for Powder Days and Storm Chasing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Chasing powder this winter? These tester-favorite skis, boots, shell, goggles and avalanche gear keep you dry, safe and skiing deep all storm cycle long. (Photo: Ray J Gadd)

Storm chasing is what most skiers dream about. One minute you’re scrolling the forecast from your desk, the next you’re cramming gear into a bag and packing up the car or hopping on a flight to score some freshies. It’s how we’d all love to spend our winters, sniffing out the best forecasts and bouncing between deep days around the country. With a strong, possibly historic El Niño predicted for this winter, there’s no telling exactly where the storm track will decide to unload. Nailing a good storm cycle takes patience, a little planning and a willingness to drop everything and go when the conditions allow. That, and the right gear to stay dry and comfortable all day long on the mountain—nothing kills a day faster than soaking wet mittens or fogged-up goggles.

Here’s the ski setup, storm-ready layers, and safety essentials our testers have long counted on for traveling far and wide to chase the biggest storms—plus a rolling bag to get it all there. Because the more dialed your gear is, the more time you can spend hunting for powder stashes. Pair these gear recs with SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide, the best tool for getting familiar with resorts across North America. That way, you’ll have a shortlist of options ready when the snow starts flying, wherever El Niño sends it.

If you have to choose just one ski for a powder-hunting mission, the Salomon S/Lab QST X is our top choice. With a 116-millimeter waist and freeride rocker profile, these sticks were made to float through champagne powder as well as dense, surfy snow, with a caruba and poplar wood core that’s light and lively. Flax and carbon fibers plus cork in the tip and tail keep things smooth and stable—a ski that can stand up to hard-charging freeriders but remains accessible for intermediates. Its midweight design—2,000 grams per ski at the 184 centimeter length—allows skiers to ride all day inbounds or mount up a hybrid binding for dropping out of bounds.

Even on a resort trip, it’s nice to keep your options open. If your plan is to primarily ski inbounds with a few short tours, the Salomon S/Lab Shift 2 10 MN Bindings are your ticket to ultimate flexibility. Salomon redesigned the Shift bindings this year, beefing up the construction in the heel and toe to help prevent pre-release and boost durability. On snow, most skiers won’t notice a big sacrifice compared with a traditional alpine binding, and you get the added benefit of a tour-capable binding perfect for a quick tour when the terrain across the valley beckons.

No one wants to tote around a second pair of boots on a ski trip. Tecnica’s new Zero G Decoy Pro boots are powerful hybrids, an ideal one-boot solution for deep trips. The Decoy delivers solid inbounds performance thanks to a stiff 130 flex, and the walk-mode lever is easy to flip with gloves on, making it simple to power up a bootpack or skintrack—or just cruise around the base area without killing your feet.

For deep days inbounds and in the backcountry, the 3-layer PowSlayer jacket and pants—available in men’s and women’s—provide ample protection without weighing you down. Powder days are full of temperature swings, and the PowSlayer kit uses a Gore-Tex ePE membrane, which repels moisture while regulating your body temp as you transition from frigid summits to top-to-bottom runs. The jacket sports a cinchable storm hood for blustery lift rides, and the pants feature a sewn-in pocket for stowing a transceiver securely.

Visibility is often limited on the deep days we dream of, and high-performance goggles become more crucial than ever. Smith’s 4D MAG ChromaPop Goggles with an extra lens offer a large field of view and the option of a photochromic lens, which is ideal on days when the light flows in and out as a storm moves through. Lens swapping is easy with these—a magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out during a quick gondola ride.

For deep days when it feels like fresh snow is sneaking into every little crevice, cinch up Black Diamond’s Mercury Mittens and consider the problem solved. A toasty fleece-lined gauntlet design delivers ample coverage while you explore the white room, and a waterproof BD.dry insert keeps your hands dry all day long. Synthetic insulation is low-profile, and the 4-way stretch shell provides a comfortable fit that lets you grip your poles securely.

An extra neckwarmer is crucial for storm skiing, and having a dry one on hand to swap in midday can easily add a few extra hours to your day. Skida’s Alpine Neckwarmer provides cozy relief from frigid wind, with a stretchy polyester shell that sheds moisture, and a fleece lining that’s like a hug for your face. The Alpine Neckwarmer is ideal for those uber-chilly powder days, while a lighter option such as the Snow Tour can be great for warmer PNW storms.

Low-profile yet spacious, the Dakine Heli Pro 20L Backpack is compact enough to ride chairs all day, with enough space for shorter ski tours and out-of-bounds laps. There’s a dedicated safety pocket to stash your shovel and probe, as well as a fleece-lined goggle pocket to protect your goggles while you hike, or keep an extra lens on hand for fogging emergencies. There are both diagonal and A-frame carry options, so it’s easy to stow your skis for quick bootpacks.

A beacon is a necessity for skiing out of bounds, and it’s never a bad idea to switch yours on for deep days at the resort as well. The industry-leading beacon for professionals and advanced skiers alike, Mammut’s Barryvox S2 Beacon features all the bells and whistles you’d want out of a pro-level device: Group Check modes, an advanced flagging feature and a 70-meter range. Recent updates include a high-contrast display and Rescue Send, which switches itself back into send mode if you’ve been still for four minutes or more.

Hauling your gear for a ski trip can feel like a hassle, and the Backcountry BGA Cottonwood Double Ski and Snowboard Rolling Bag makes the process smoother. With a unique roll-top design, the padded bag can hold skis up to 195 centimeters—but easily rolls smaller if you don’t need the space—and internal and external storage pockets are perfect for stashing dirty socks for the way home. It’s spacious enough to fit two pairs of skis plus ample gear, and the durable 840-denier polyester and nylon construction stands up to years of wear and tear.
