#8198. New Climbing Gym in Massachusetts Plans to Give Away All Its Profits

Berkshire Boulders General Manager Austen McNulty (left) and founder Nick Friedman (right) inside the gym. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Friedman)

The United States has become known for corporate climbing gyms and nationwide chains fraught with labor issues that charge high dollar. A recent analysis by an adventure travel company, which leverages 2026 data as well as the Climbing Business Journal’s 2025 trends report, declared that “the United States is the industry’s laboratory” when it comes to mega-gyms backed by private equity. As climbing becomes more popular, and thus more profitable, one may question whether these gyms will inevitably become the norm.

But in Great Barrington, a small town of a little more than 7,000 residents in Western Massachusetts, entrepreneur Nick Friedman is moving in the opposite direction: starting a new, independent gym that gives away all its profits.

You can trace the 38-year-old’s vision for an altruistic gym back to his childhood, when his dad put his career on hold to demand that General Electric clean up the river that ran through town—and Friedman’s property. In the 1970s, General Electric dumped polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the Housatonic River, so Friedman’s dad fought to hold the company liable. GE settled, paying $250 million.

In the process, Friedman learned the importance of activism. The cause close to Friedman’s heart is climbing access, which is not exactly easy to come by in Great Barrington or the Berkshires—but not for a lack of rock. While he calls the climbing in Great Barrington world-class, he says that privately owned land and conservation organizations that don’t understand the value of climbing make access a problem.

“Great Barrington is this unique case study in incredible climbing that is barred from true public domain due to land access challenges,” said Friedman, who has been deeply involved in local access work. In 2023, Friedman, who also serves on the board of the Western Massachusetts Climbers’ Coalition (WMCC), purchased a 70-acre parcel in the Farley Ledges climbing area. This bought WMCC time to organize the permits and funding to purchase it from Friedman earlier this year. While Farley Ledges currently remains closed due to an access issue involving a private landowner, WMCC is raising funds to construct a new parking lot and trail to reopen climbing.

Making these land purchases and forging the agreements necessary to maintain and expand access in Western Massachusetts takes a lot of resources, Friedman explains. That’s where his new gym, Berkshire Boulders, which opens on November 6, comes in. He plans to donate 100% of his profits to community organizations, including WMCC and Access Fund.

“The WMCC is very excited about the opening of Berkshire Boulders and the potential it has to positively impact climbing access in Western Massachusetts,” said Regina Madden, a WMCC board member and chair of its communications committee. Protecting and maintaining access requires ongoing resources, so a local business committed to supporting that mission creates an excellent opportunity. In addition, Berkshire Boulders can serve to bridge the gap between indoor and outdoor climbing, helping to foster a stronger sense of stewardship and community.

While Friedman may pursue nonprofit status down the line, he says it was faster to get the gym off the ground as a business that gave away its profits, rather than a 501(c)3 nonprofit. And as someone who has specialized professionally in startups, he adds that he’s always been “intrigued” by hybrid models that blend for-profit business models with nonprofit values.

Currently, the organizations Berkshire Boulders plans to support include WMCC and Access Fund, as well as non-climbing local organizations including the Railroad Street Youth Project and Greenagers, which fosters sustainability work among youth.

“I felt that a climbing gym could play a central role in that effort and become this anchor and the starting point for a broader vision of bringing outdoor recreation more front and center in this small town,” Friedman said.

Friedman doesn’t see accessibility as a binary, “indoors or outdoors” issue; he views it holistically. This is why he’s made it the gym’s mission to improve climbing access indoors and out. He envisions a gym as a place where you can learn the sport, meet partners, and find people to help you make the gym-to-crag transition. In Friedman’s view, that gym-to-crag transition is the end game. That’s why he decorated Berkshire Boulders’ walls with photographs of Great Barrington rock, and rents out crashpads to climbers who want to try bouldering outside, but lack the gear.

But the other end game is community, which he says is hard to foster when you’re answering to private equity investors. Berkshire Boulders’ KPIs will instead revolve “around community impact.”

One way he’s doing that is by offering hardship memberships. Each month, Berkshire Boulders will award free memberships to low-income individuals through a lottery system. This addresses the known problem of affordability in the gym industry—one so notable that the American Alpine Club declared it an access issue in 2024. Friedman says he’s already approved one hardship membership application, but doesn’t have a monthly quota in mind yet. “We do expect to expand that program significantly over the next several months,” Friedman said.

A focus on community KPIs, however, will not come at the expense of a high-quality bouldering facility. Friedman insists that he is committed to a top-tier facility. He is partnering with local hold-maker Decoy and plans to change the setting across the 15-foot-high walls every two weeks. The gym also features a custom-built, “artistically created” adjustable spray wall. Using the Clift app, climbers will be able to set sequences, replicate local outdoor problems, and track leaderboards.

Currently, for Friedman, Berkshire Boulders is a passion project. His personal endgame is not to make a living off the gym—he still works full-time as the chief strategy officer at a small-batch cannabis startup. He also hired an experienced general manager to run the gym. Rather, that Friedman hopes to ultimately do is drive positive change in his local climbing community.

“Personally, I would love to see the Great Barrington climbing become a published resource for the public,” Friedman said. It’s a long game, but a worthy one, in his view, to turn the local climbing from an underground, tricky access dance to a veritable destination with routes documented on Mountain Project, a guidebook, and formal parking and approach trails.

Beyond local impact, could Berkshire Boulders, if successful, inspire a rising tide of small, mission-driven gyms in this era of indoor climbing corporatization? Friedman believes smaller gyms with a focus on community have a better shot at bringing together passionate climbers than the larger conglomerate gyms. “I would love to see an expansion of smaller independent gyms regionally,” he says.

#8197. A River Runs Through It. An AI Data Center Tried to Move In.

Anglers enjoy the iconic Blackfoot River in Montana, known for its blue ribbon trout fishing (Photo: Matt Roberts)

Brenna Love grew up fishing on the Blackfoot, a snow-fed Montana mountain river that spans 130 miles from its headwaters on the Continental Divide to the confluence of the Clark Fork River, seven miles east of Missoula. Its cold, fast-flowing water makes for premier blue ribbon trout fishing, scenic canyons, and whitewater recreation.

The Blackfoot was immortalized in Norman Maclean’s 1976 book A River Runs Through It and Other Stories, which was turned into a Hollywood film starring Brad Pitt in 1992.

Love, 29, is a resident of Bonner, a former mill town with just 2,700 residents located along the banks of the Blackfoot.

“My earliest memories are on my family’s raft,” Love told Outside. “Every time you’re on the water, you’re surrounded by other people loving the same backyard that we love so deeply. You look around and see people on boats of all shapes, sizes, and colors, recreating and enjoying. It’s the reason we live here in Montana.”

In March of 2026, an Idaho-based technology company called Krambu announced plans to build an artificial intelligence data center in Bonner, just steps from the banks of the Blackfoot. The project would convert an old mill building into a warehouse for computer servers, and the complex would draw water from the nearby Blackfoot River to provide continuous cooling for the computer racks.

Love and her community fought back—and won.

“It was hard,” she told Outside. “It was really hard. It took organizing and talking with each other about what this means. It took our evenings, our lunch breaks, reviewing the new application materials and doing our own research.”

It’s the latest in a growing wave of community pushback against big tech’s data center expansion—and a reminder that local voices, when organized, can have a lasting impact.

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

According to Public Lands Intelligence, as of this writing, 1,302 data centers are proposed or under construction, in addition to 904 already operating across 49 states and Washington, D.C.

But as construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in towns and cities. The centers are often loud and large, and they eat up valuable electricity. As data centers have faced bipartisan backlash in cities across the country, tech firms have looked to rural communities, farming towns, and even unused public land to build.

At least 35 of current data center applications are on public lands, the Center for Western Priorities reports, and some are directly adjacent to national park units.

Secretary of the Department of the Interior Doug Burgum has tens of millions invested in AI data centers, according to a report published by ProPublica. In September, The Washington Sun reported that the Trump administration was considering at least 12 data center-related infrastructure projects on federal public lands.

Private equity firm Blackstone is building the Tallgrass Energy Project, a massive AI data center located south of Cheyenne, Wyoming. Blackstone also backed a historic $105 million donation to Yellowstone National Park.

The list goes on. Roughly 115 miles from Yellowstone’s north entrance, Quantica’s Big Sky Campus is proposing a 5,100-acre, or nearly eight-square-mile, data center. In Kentucky, Cave Point Commerce Center is a proposed 381-acre hyperscale data center near Mammoth Cave National Park. The City of Page, Arizona, is considering a $10 billion data center two miles from Horseshoe Bend near Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. In July, the federal government fast-tracked a data center ten miles from Lake Mead.

In Bonner, the proposed data center would be in the Bonner Mill, a historic 169-acre former lumber mill along the riverbank. Originally built in 1886, the sawmill closed in 2008 and was transformed in 2011 into a multi-tenant industrial park.

Ben Catton, a legislative assistant at the Montana Environmental Information Center (MEIC), told Outside that sites like the Bonner Mill are ideal for companies that build data centers.

“Tech companies target old mill sites,” Catton said. “That’s part of their business model: to look for this existing infrastructure. Because those were really energy-consumptive sites, they have a lot of that energy infrastructure in place already.”

According to the Krambu proposal, the Bonner Mill data center would draw 16 million gallons of water from the river in July and August to cool its servers. Under Catton’s calculations, that means the 240,000-square-foot center would require roughly one megawatt of power—enough to power 800 homes for a year.

Montana’s energy and water needs during its driest months didn’t sit well with him.

“They’re going to be very consumptive in the two months when the landscape is the thirstiest for that water, when our rivers are at their lowest, and when our fish are most in need of cold water,” Catton said.

The Bonner Mill sits 100 yards from Love’s front porch, and as a concerned community member, she began reaching out to her neighbors one by one to discuss the plan.

“Start by having a conversation with your neighbor, and then your other neighbor, and then your other neighbor,” Love said. “Those conversations really build up to a community-wide conversation.”

On March 20, local nonprofit Friends of Two Rivers—so-named for the confluence of the Clark Fork and Blackfoot Rivers—hosted the first public meeting at Saint Ann Catholic Church, a rural, single-story neighborhood church originally built in 1905. Against a wood-paneled backdrop, representatives from Krambu and Missoula County, along with Bonner Mill property manager Mike Heisey, spoke on a panel to a standing-room-only crowd.

Organizers were surprised by how many people showed up, Love recalled. Most people were there to voice their concerns about the project.

“There were just so many different people engaging in so many different ways through different avenues, and that’s what eventually changed the tide,” Love said. “It was organized in all of these different pockets, and I think any one of those groups couldn’t have done it alone.”

It was the first of many meetings held at libraries, schools, in living rooms, and at coffee shops. Love said she participated in at least eight, primarily working with her HOA members in closed meetings, as well as informal working groups of neighbors and the managers of the Bonner Milltown Historical Center.

“Rather than a scattershot signs and flyers approach, we were trying to find avenues where we thought we could make an impact,” Love said. “We organized as our HOA and then submitted our concerns and questions directly to the property manager.”

Love is one of hundreds who rallied through social media and in person to oppose the data center. Local regulations at the time weren’t rigid enough to deny Krambu approval, so Love and her team took their concerns directly to the property manager.

“The more direct action and impact you can make, the better,” Love said. “If you can figure out who has the authority, whether it is your county or your city, via the regulations in place there, the owner of the site, or who has investment in the community, find them.”

Between March and June of 2026, Krambu submitted five iterations of its application to build the data center, each time drawing backlash from the community. Love and other local advocates launched a petition that garnered more than 50,000 signatories to reject the AI data center, and flooded every town meeting with shoulder-to-shoulder opposition.

Citing overwhelming public feedback and neighborhood opposition, Heisey officially announced on July 6, 2026, that the property would not move forward with the data center and withdrew his support for the application.

A Krambu spokesperson told Outside in a statement that the company is under new leadership and that the Bonner data center was spearheaded by the company’s former management. The company has no plans to revisit the Bonner project, the spokesperson said.

In direct response to the community concerns exposed during the Krambu review, Missoula County Commissioners approved a temporary one-year moratorium on July 9 on new zoning permits for large-scale data centers to establish more comprehensive regulatory frameworks.

Love credits the victory to her community’s ability to organize across multiple fronts: viral online opposition, petitions, public comments and meeting attendance, coordinated feedback from small groups and the HOA, and direct outreach to decision-makers, from county commissioners and city council members to the landowner.

It’s a big win for a small mountain town, and one that could pave the way for other rural areas facing data center proposals.

Montana is perhaps uniquely positioned for these types of fights. The Montana Constitution enshrines the right to a “clean and healthful environment” as a fundamental right, requiring the state and individuals to maintain and improve the environment for present and future generations. Outdoor recreation is also a major economic input for Montana, contributing $3.8 billion to the Montana economy.

Adam Schellhammer, Mid-Atlantic regional director for the nonprofit advocacy group American Rivers, warns that data centers pose new threats to states without such incentives or protections.

“On the national level, trends show that the speed and scale of development is just ramping up so quickly that we’re just having trouble keeping up,” Schellhammer said.

According to Schellhammer, data center regulation is fragmented across federal, state, and local municipal agencies. Water usage details are frequently concealed under non-disclosure agreements or classified as proprietary corporate information. Because many areas do not legally mandate public disclosure, city planners cannot always establish accurate water budgets to understand a center’s full impact. Schellhammer says communities should start by updating industrial zoning and land-use ordinances to make a difference, rather than reacting after sites are chosen.

“The lesson learned is that every single voice matters,” Love said. “If there’s something you care about, say so. Find a place to speak your truth, speak your concerns, be an advocate for the things that you are passionate about, and someone will hear you.”

#8196. The Best Low-Volume Ski Boots for Narrow Feet, Tested

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Six narrow-last boots for slim feet, low insteps, and skinny calves, from Lange, Salomon, Nordica, Rossignol, and Tecnica. (Photo: Keri Bascetta)

Overview: The best ski boots for narrow feet are low-volume models with lasts of 97 to 98 mm. Our picks are the Lange Shadow LV, Lange Code 130 LV BOA, Salomon S/Pro Alpha C BOA, Nordica Promachine 3, Rossignol Hi-Speed Elite LV, and Tecnica Mach1 LV 130, with most priced between $550 and $950.

Skiers with narrow feet have a unique problem when it comes to shopping for ski boots. While bootfitters can easily grind, punch, and stretch shells and liners to better accommodate wide feet, it’s more difficult for them to fill up space in a boot to get a narrow foot and heel to stay put. That’s why getting the fit right off the wall matters even more for skiers with narrow feet.

If your feet, ankle, heel, and calf are slim—or your instep low—chances are you’re a candidate for a low-volume boot with a last of around 98 millimeters. It used to be that only a handful of brands made low-volume boots that weren’t the vice grips racers wear on the World Cup circuit. Fortunately, that’s changed. These days, skiers with narrow feet have an abundance of low-volume, narrow-lasted options across flex ranges. Here are the picks our boot testers recommend for 2027.

Last: 97 mm Flexes: 140, 130, 120, 110 (men’s); 115, 95 (women’s) Sizes: 24.5–31.5

Pros and Cons + Extremely responsive flex + Snug heel pockets for high-performance fit – Generic Velcro power strap may not be strong enough for expert skiers

The Shadow series replaced Lange’s long-running RX line, and the payoff for narrow feet is in the fit. If you felt the old RX heel was too wide and blocky, the Shadow LV’s snugged-up heel pocket will put a smile on your face. The forefoot is winnowed down, and the medial wall skips the RX’s familiar navicular and ankle-bone pressure. The instep stays generous, but the liner’s auxetic shaping and reduced material over the cuneiform bones kept us secure without feeling like we were swimming. On snow, the Suspension Blade (a boltless, overlapping spine) and the Dual Pivot send force through the sole to the tip of the ski. The flex curve is much steeper than the RX’s long, slow one: almost any pressure on the tongue drives the shovel, and a few of us found it almost twitchy on a 70-millimter-waisted cheater slalom ski. In longer turns it felt plush and powerful, with resounding feedback in deep powder. Our one gripe: a generic Velcro power strap on a boot this luxe.

Last: 98 mm Flexes: 130, 110 (men’s); 115, 95, 85 (women’s) Sizes: 22–30.5

Pros and Cons + Much easier entry than previous narrow model + Very snug but well-contoured low-volume fit + Highly tactile edging feel and responsiveness – Long-travel flex feel may take getting used to

The all-new Salomon S/Pro Alpha C BOA is a tight boot—old-school narrow—but shaped in a modern way that accounts for the foot’s natural curves and bony spots rather than fighting them. Testers were struck by how easily the foot slid into such a snug shell, unusually easy entry and exit for a narrow-fitting boot, and they loved the fit and feel of the cuff-only BOA closure. But the most notable feature of this boot is the new shell design: it lacks a traditional cuff attachment and pivot point on the inner ankle. The cuff curves smoothly around the ankle with no screws or rivets in sight and anchors low near the sole with two screws and a small metal plate called Powerlink. That low connection creates a direct line from leg to ski edge, with a longer flex feel that took some of us a bit to adjust to. Once we did, we were won over by the connection to the edge and the sensitivity underfoot at any speed.

Last: 98 mm Flexes: 130, 120 (men’s); 115, 95 (women’s) Sizes: 22.5–30.5

Pros and Cons + New 3Force shell is lighter and stiffer for better responsiveness + New lace-up liner improves fit for slender legs + Still one of the tightest fits but avoids hotspots – Lace-up liner makes entry more difficult

The Promachine was the last of the Nordica Machine family to get a “3,” probably because the old boot didn’t need fixing. For low-volume skiers who want more performance, the wait paid off. The new 3Force Frame—a light, stiff skeleton co-molded into the softer polyurethane of the lower shell—sharpens energy transfer and cuts weight, while the shell shape barely changed. That’s good news if you have narrow feet: with its 98-millimeter last, this is still one of the snuggest all-mountain boots on the market, and we were impressed by how free of hotspots the fit stays. The 130-flex model also gets a lace-up version of the cork-lined liner that tightens the instep and lower leg. We loved the extra containment—less so the harder entry—but for slender-legged skiers chasing a gap-free fit, it’s worth the hassle.

Last: 98 mm Flexes: 140, 120 Sizes: 24.5–31.5

Pros and Cons + Precise fit and feel matches on-snow experience + More snug fit throughout than previous version + Updated liner offers less pack-out – Only available in two flex models

The Rossignol Hi-Speed Elite LV isn’t an all-new boot, but a few key updates make it a better one—and a better fit for narrow feet. The 140 flex we tested (a 120 is also available) is stiffer than before, but the real gains come from the new R-Go Fit liner. Different foams around the heel and ankle give more sculpted grip and a 15 percent cut in pack-out where it matters most. A thicker, more textured sock-side material kept us firmly in place without the slippery feel of past versions. A thin, rubberized polyurethane film on the liner’s exterior also helps it mold tighter to the shell. It might sound like liner-ado about nothing, but several of us said it made a bigger difference than most full shell redesigns we test in a year. We called it the perfect narrow boot: firm, snug, and consistent in feel, flex, and power. What you feel at try-on matches what you get on snow, no molding session required.

Last: 97 mm (also 100 mm) Flex: 140, 130, 120 (men’s); 115, 95 (women’s) Sizes: 23.5-29.5

Pros and Cons + Excellent low-volume fit + Damp and powerful + Responsive flex shines in both the resort and the backcountry – Heavy, with poor range of motion

The Lange Code 130 LV is a true low-volume boot in an 80/20 package: a boot worn inbounds most of the time that can sneak out a gate, skin back to the base area, or, frankly, be a little more comfortable on the dance floor. It replaces the much-loved XT3, and the narrow fit is the headline—the anatomical liner provided stellar heel hold and really locked our tester’s foot in. Don’t knock its skiing chops, though. He reported top-tier precision on piste, thanks (he thinks) to the Active Blade in the spine, which made the boot feel almost like it had a bolted spine rather than a walk-mode lever. Dual Core plastic delivered the classic Lange damping, especially on a walk outside Kirkwood where spring powder had set up sooner than he anticipated. The trade-off: a 1,910-gram boot with 54 degrees of range of motion isn’t the best bet for climbing 6,000 vertical feet or banging out lap after lap in a secret stash. But for skiers who want one narrow boot to ski a few laps out of bounds and hammer bumps or groomers all day, the Code is an excellent bet.

Last: 98 mm Flex: 130, 120 (men’s)’ 115, 95 (women’s) Sizes: 22.5–30.5

Pros and Cons + More room in toebox + Snappy rebound + Improved frontside performance – Not as damp as previous version

The previous Mach1 LV was the lowest-volume, 98mm-lasted boot on the market, a favorite of expert skiers with narrow feet who didn’t mind some time in the boot shop. The newest update still has a low-volume, 98-millimeter last, but it’s the most forgiving fit here. Our tester, who has logged well over 300 days in the old boot, says Tecnica raised the toebox ceiling—the old one left his big toe unable to move, even with the thinnest sock—and opened the heel pocket a fair bit wider below the Achilles. He felt no heel movement to speak of, and the stock liner is still one of the best on the market for fit and ease of customization. The new T-Drive and carbon-coinjected cuff give a snappier rebound from the bottom of the flex, and on his “janky kitchen scale,” the boot weighs almost 100 grams less than the previous model. The trade-off is damping: it’s palpably less damp off-piste than the old Mach1. He still calls it a best-in-class all-mountain boot, just one with a balance shifted toward the frontside.

Fit makes or breaks a ski boot, and narrow feet make it harder to get right, because a boot that’s too roomy is tough to fix. Expert skiers vetted and tested every boot here, but the best one for you depends on your own feet. A professional bootfitter is still the fastest way to narrow the field. Until you get there, here’s what to know.

Boot width is listed as the last: the internal width at the forefoot, in millimeters, measured on a size 26/26.5 shell. The number also hints at overall volume—the height over your instep and the room around your lower leg in the cuff. Narrower boots generally have a lower instep and a snugger cuff, while wider boots have a higher instep and a roomier cuff. Boots sort into three groups:

Every boot in this guide is a low-volume model, with lasts of 97 to 98mm.

Not always. Some skiers with narrower feet are comfortable in a medium-volume boot. A bootfitter can stretch a shell more easily than fill one, though, so a boot that’s too roomy is harder to fix than one that’s too snug. Everyone’s tolerance for a snug fit differs, so try several widths at a ski shop and go with what your feet tell you.

Feet and legs come in too many shapes for one tester to speak for everyone. A boot that feels custom-made on one skier can feel punishing on another. That’s why we partner with professional bootfitter Mark Elling, who leads the Masterfit/America’s Best Bootfitters annual ski boot test. Every brand, large or small, is invited to submit models. Over two weeks, 10 expert testers—evenly split between men and women—skied 50 boots, averaging three runs per boot across a range of conditions. For this guide, we pulled the low-volume boots with lasts under 100mm from SKI’s tests and reviews.

Mark Elling has worked full-time in the ski industry for more than 35 years as a writer, a level 3 PSIA-certified instructor, a snowcat skiing guide and a professional bootfitter. He runs a year-round specialty bootfitting lab in Bend, Oregon (BootRX.com), and is a former board-certified pedorthist. Elling coordinates Masterfit’s annual boot test, and he’s the author of The All-Mountain Skier: The Way to Expert Skiing.

#8195. Calling Washington Backpackers: This $5,000 Grant Could Fund Your PCT Thru-Hike

Walking may be free, but a thru-hike is decidedly expensive: Some Pacific Crest Trail trekkers run up a bill north of $10,000 during a months-long hike. That cost, plus the need to take off work for half a year, presents massive barriers to many would-be thru-hikers.

Seattleite Geoff Burg knows this—and he wants to help. With fellow Washington hikers Keya Gillenwater and Madelyn Scherrer, Burg launched the Pacific Crest Trail Grant in 2025 to award $5,000 to a Washington-based hiker with dreams of completing the trail.

Burg’s connection to the PCT goes back a decade. The attorney was hiking with his kids near Stevens Pass in 2016 when he came across some hikers in distress. Burg volunteered to drive the duo, a pair of PCT thru-hikers in their 60s, into town for medical supplies, then offered them a place to stay in his family’s home. The couple told Burg all about their thru-hike and ultralight philosophy—and the encounter stuck with him.

Over the next several years, Burg chipped away at a section hike of the Washington segment of the PCT. He fell in love with being on the trail, alone or with his kids, and with the greater hiking community around it. Several years later, a conversation with his massage therapist sparked the idea of a scholarship. Well established in his career, and with experience as an advisor for a youth outdoor leadership program, Burg was in a position to help others achieve their long trail dreams.

“We give scholarships for football and baseball and everything else,” he says. “Why not for hiking?”

So he connected with former mentees Gillenwater and Scherrer, a PCT alum, and formed a committee. The grant would offer financial support to a young Washingtonian hoping to complete the long trail.

Burg especially wanted to support young hikers with a financial need; applicants must be between the ages of 18 and 33, with strong ties to Washington state. They should also be able to demonstrate past backpacking experience, which Burg hopes will improve the recipient’s chances of succeeding on a thru-hike and paying the experience forward through volunteer projects like youth outreach or LNT education. Grant recipients who meet that criteria are chosen via a lottery, and must stay in touch with the grant committee during their hikes. Burg emphasizes that the process is not merit-based.

“We already have a community of people that can do this or who want to do this, but within that broader community, there’s so many people that can’t afford it,” he says.

Thirty-two-year-old Seattleite Kayla Provost was the grant’s first recipient. She completed her trek in September 2026, and says she couldn’t have finished the thru-hike without the financial support.

Provost had previously worked as a naturalist guide and, as a Washington resident, felt deeply connected to the Cascades. After losing her mom a few years prior, Provost felt compelled to change her lifestyle. She felt called to the PCT, but financial hurdles posed challenges. After searching “grants for thru-hiking” online, Provost stumbled across a Reddit post about the PCT Grant.

“The grant was truly a lifeline for me,” she says. “Beyond the financial support, the monthly check-ins with the grant committee gave me a sense of accountability and reminded me I had people cheering me on.”

She says the experience redoubled her desire to facilitate outdoor experiences for other people.

“It is incredibly powerful to make a choice, trust yourself enough to follow through, and learn to be comfortable with the uncomfortable,” she says. “The trail offered me a deep sense of confidence, gratitude, and trust in my own ability to navigate the unknown.”

The grant will fund its second thru-hiker in 2027. Through donations, Burg hopes to grow the program into a self-sustaining fund to support more hikers on more trails.

Applications for prospective 2027 PCT thru-hikers are currently open. Washingtonians who meet the criteria can apply by January 31.

#8194. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

Those gorgeous flowers are months away, but their buds are already waiting. The right fall care can make all the difference when warmer days return.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Azaleas and rhododendrons paint the spring garden in gorgeous shades of pink, red, orange, and other vibrant colors. But the work of protecting those future flowers starts now. Fall care before winter is essential for keeping these shrubs healthy and ready to bloom abundantly in spring.

Fall azalea care and rhododendron care are all about preparing them for winter dormancy, maintaining healthy roots, and protecting flower buds. Did you know that these shrubs form their buds in summer? Next year’s flowers are already set in buds, so now is the time to preserve and protect them.

Azaleas and rhododendrons are very similar plants with similar care needs in fall. However, keep in mind that there are deciduous and evergreen types with slightly different needs. We’ll point these out here, along with the essential tasks you should be tackling this fall for all your Rhododendron species.

Fall is not the time for heavy annual pruning of rhododendrons or azaleas. Most spring-blooming members of this plant flower on old growth. This means they set buds over the summer. Trimming too hard in the fall will prune away many of the buds that become next spring’s flowers.

The best time for heavy shaping or pruning is right after spring flowering. But this doesn’t mean you can’t or shouldn’t make any cuts in fall. Inspect your shrubs now for dead, damaged, or diseased branches. Remove these using sharp, clean bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8, available on Amazon, which can cut through woody stems up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. For larger branches, switch to loppers or a pruning saw.

Fertilizing late in the season can trigger new growth that only gets damaged in winter conditions. That damage can introduce disease. It’s also a waste of energy that should be going into keeping roots healthy over winter.

Most fertilizing for azaleas and rhododendrons takes place in spring, after flowering. At that time, you can use a product formulated specifically for these shrubs or for any acid-loving shrub. Also, consider the fact that your shrubs might not need feeding at all if they are healthy or thriving.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you suspect your plants need fertilizer, a soil test is the best way to determine their nutrient needs. The MySoil Soil Test Kit measures both soil pH and nutrient levels, helping you identify any deficiencies before deciding whether to feed your shrubs in spring.

You should keep watering your azaleas and rhododendrons right up until the ground freezes, especially if you’re having a dry autumn. Ideally, the ground will be moist before real winter weather sets in. Check the soil regularly using a moisture meter, such as the Yamron 4-in-1, to see whether water is reaching the root zone. Provide a deep soaking as needed, including one as late in the season as possible before the ground freezes.

This matters because many azaleas and rhododendrons are evergreen, making them susceptible to desiccation, or drying out, over winter. Cold, dry winds leech moisture from the leaves, but roots in frozen ground can’t take up any water. This can result in curled, brown leaves and even damaged buds. Ensuring there is moisture in the ground before winter is less important for deciduous types.

Mulch insulates the soil and roots of your flowering shrubs. It helps regulate soil temperature, retains more moisture around the roots, and prevents the root damage caused by soil heaving that occurs during cycles of freezing and thawing.

Organic mulches such as shredded pine bark or partially decomposed, shredded leaves are ideal for mulching azaleas and rhododendrons. If you don't have suitable materials to hand, Garden Pro's shredded pine bark mulch from Home Depot is a good alternative. Layer the mulch around the root zones of shrubs to a depth of 2 to 3 inches (5–8 cm). Keep it a few inches away from stems to prevent trapping moisture that can encourage rot and disease.

Moist soil is important, especially for evergreen shrubs, but too much moisture can also be damaging. Poorly drained soil can lead to root rot and fungal diseases. Eventually, these diseases can kill shrubs.

Look for signs your shrubs are getting waterlogged: standing water around plants, soggy soil long after rainfall, and wilting or yellowing foliage even when the plants have plenty of water. It’s important to try to remediate soggy conditions. You can clear off compacted mulch and other plant debris, divert runoff from other areas, or regrade the surrounding soil, for instance. If the problem isn’t easily fixed, consider relocating the plant in spring.

Evergreen azaleas and rhododendrons add beautiful color and texture to the winter garden, but they are also more vulnerable to winter damage. Winter burn happens when the leaves lose moisture faster than the roots can draw up water to replace it.

Cold and dry winter wind is a primary cause of winter burn on evergreen shrubs, so creating a windbreak can protect them from much of the damage. Set up a barrier on the side of the shrubs that get hit by winter wind, using natural burlap garden fabric, like this from Home Depot, attached to wooden stakes.

Don’t let the barrier actually touch the leaves. They need some airflow to stay healthy. Young shrubs are more likely to need this kind of winter protection. Established shrubs in more sheltered areas are probably fine without it.

Finally, it’s a good idea to look over your shrubs for any signs of problems caused by common azalea pests or diseases. Managing these issues now can prevent them from carrying over into next year’s growing season. Look for stippling or black specks on leaves, which can indicate lace bugs, a common pest of azaleas and rhododendrons. A 10x illuminated magnifying loupe, like this Carson loupe from Amazon, can help you inspect the undersides of leaves, where these tiny insects and their dark droppings are often found.

An unusual number of dying branches, persistent wilting, and many or unusual leaf spots can indicate fungal diseases and root rot. Keep in mind that some spots are normal and that leaf drop is expected in deciduous varieties.

If you do see issues or unusual damage, remove diseased plant material and dispose of it. If issues persist or you don’t know how to identify or treat a particular pest, check with your local extension office for advice.

Fall azalea and rhododendron care isn’t extensive, but it will help you protect next year’s flowers, safeguard vulnerable foliage, and keep roots healthy. Simple steps now help your shrubs enter winter in better condition and improve the chances of a healthy, colorful spring display.

Fresh grass seed can take longer to sprout than the bag suggests, especially as fall cools off. A slow start is usually normal, and a few simple changes can help it along...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is when a lot of homeowners get around to overseeding cool-season lawns. You rake out the thin spots, spread the seed and set the sprinkler going. Two weeks later, plenty of those patches still look like bare dirt, and it's tempting to blame the seed.

Chances are, the seed is fine. Anyone who has spent time seeding a lawn knows some grasses are just slow, and a couple of the usual fall picks can take weeks to show anything. Fall is still a smart time to seed, though. The ground stays warm from summer while the air cools off, and the rain usually picks back up.

Grab the bag and check what's in it. A blend might mix ryegrass, fescue and bluegrass, and those don't keep the same schedule. Ryegrass can be up in about a week, while bluegrass may take a month, so a new blend looks spotty at first. And green doesn't mean done – new grass still needs several more weeks to root in.

The rest happens underground. Cool-season seed generally won't germinate until the soil is above about 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and colder ground can leave it sitting there until spring. Push a soil thermometer (like this one from the Urban Worm Store) in to see where yours is. The seed also has to stay damp and reach dirt, not just rest on dead thatch.

Any lawn that slows down and browns a little in July, then greens back up when the nights cool off, is a cool-season lawn. Bermuda, zoysia and bahiagrass are the opposite; those warm-season grasses do better seeded in late spring or early summer, after the soil has warmed up.

Across the upper Midwest and other northern areas, the ground cools early, so the window runs from mid-August to mid-September and has usually closed by October. Farther south, in places like Tennessee, there's room to seed into mid-October. Anything sown late has less time to get established before the first hard freeze.

Perennial ryegrass is what you want when a bare spot has to look green before winter – a worn strip by the mailbox, let's say, or the patch where the dog cuts across the yard. It's often up in 5 to 10 days. Sow it early in the fall window. One option is Pennington Fairway Supreme perennial ryegrass from Lowe's, which comes in a 50-pound bag with fertilizer mixed in. It's at its best in cool, moist weather and doesn't take drought well. In the South, it mostly gets sown over dormant Bermuda for winter color, not as a permanent lawn.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your USDA Planting Zone is somewhere between Kansas and the Carolinas, your lawn may well be tall fescue already. Bluegrass struggles in those hot summers, but fescue's deep roots carry it through dry spells. Seed usually comes up within a week or two. GreenView turf-type tall fescue seed, available on Amazon, comes in 7-pound bags. Fescue grows in clumps rather than spreading, though, so thin spots won't fill in by themselves and need reseeding in early to mid-fall.

Bluegrass asks for patience up front. It usually takes at least two weeks to sprout and can take closer to a month. Once it's up, it spreads by underground rhizomes into a thick, soft lawn that can fill worn spots back in. It does best where summers stay fairly cool. Get it down right at the start of your fall window. Home Depot stocks a 5.6-pound bag of Scotts Turf Builder Kentucky bluegrass mix.

Keen for your grass to get a move on? Look this way...

Get down and look closely at a patch that still hasn't come up. You'll often find the seed sitting on top of old thatch or dead leaves instead of on the soil. It dries out between waterings up there; indeed, its first root may never reach the soil. Before you seed, mow the grass you already have down to about 1 1/2 to 2 inches (4–5cm), rake out the loose debris, then scratch up the surface until you can see bare, crumbly soil.

On small areas, a stiff 16-tine steel bow rake like the one Walmart carries will break up a crusted surface. Once the seed is down, rake over it lightly to work it into the top 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3–6mm) of soil, or press it in with the back of the rake. Don't worry if some seed is still showing, since bluegrass actually sprouts better with a little light.

On a breezy afternoon, soil watered at breakfast can be pale and crusty by the evening. Seed that's begun to swell can dry out and fail. Short, light sprinkles once or twice a day, and one more on days like that, keep the top inch (2.5cm) damp, not muddy. Long soaks can float seed into low spots or waterlog the soil, and an overnight rain counts as a turn.

A pulsing impact head can knock seed loose, but an oscillating sprinkler lays water down in a soft sweep. With the Melnor XT turbo oscillating sprinkler from Amazon, you can narrow the spray so it stays on the seed, not the sidewalk. For days when nobody's home, the Orbit single-outlet hose faucet timer from Home Depot can run short cycles as often as once an hour. Once seedlings have roots, water less often but more deeply.

A thin layer of screened compost over the seed helps keep the surface from drying out so fast. That layer gives the seed some protection from heavy rain, too. Spread it no more than about 1/4 inch (6mm) deep. You should still be able to see a little seed and soil through it.

Thicker isn't better. Grass seed carries only a small store of energy, and seed buried too deep can use it up before the shoot reaches light —, and fine bluegrass seed may not sprout under a heavy layer at all.

If you don't have finished compost, a bag of Scotts Turf Builder lawn soil from Home Depot is made for overseeding and top dressing.

So how long should you wait? With ryegrass or tall fescue in soil that's stayed warm and damp, about three weeks is a fair wait. Before reseeding, scrape back a little soil and look. Swollen or split seed is still working, while seed that looks dry and unchanged probably dried out or never touched the soil. Old seed can be the culprit too, so check the packaging date.

Don't count on starter fertilizer to hurry any of this along. Seed carries its own food for germination, and starter fertilizer is there to feed seedlings once roots form – too much can burn tender new grass. If your fall window has closed, it's better to stop than to keep sowing into cold soil. Some people dormant seed instead, spreading it in late fall once the soil is too cold for sprouting but before the ground freezes. Otherwise, early next fall is the more reliable time to try again.

Slow grass seed usually just needs a few more weeks. Choose the right grass for your area, sow it while the soil is still warm, and keep it damp. That will do more than any quick fix. With some patience, those bare spots may be filled in by the time you mow next spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

From Venus flytraps to corkscrew plants, your birth month carnivorous plant might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On paper, birth month carnivorous plants sounds... well, a little twisted, especially when you compare it to the usual birth month flowers. Most of us have a side to our personality that we don't show the world every day, though, and these plants are the perfect way to shine a light on our dark side.

These remarkable plants are far from ordinary. From the Venus flytrap's sudden snapping jaws to pitcher plants luring in unsuspecting insects, carnivorous plants have developed some ingenious ways to survive. Some are bold and imposing, others are subtle and deceptive, and each and every single one has its own strategy for getting what it needs.

So how does this tie into you? Well, from birth month birds to birth month animals, nature offers us countless ways to reflect on our character. The lens of carnivorous plants, though? Why, that adds a much more intriguing twist! Behind ambition, for example, there may be a need for control. Sensitivity can sometimes turn into possessiveness, while confidence can tip into arrogance. Even our most admirable qualities can have a less flattering side... and there's no point denying it.

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month owl, birth month tree, and birth month spider (oh yes, I'm deadly serious!), but carnivorous plants perfectly pair with the traits, instincts and impulses that sit beneath the surface of your everyday personality.

You might be determined to the point of stubborn, much like the Venus flytrap; you might, like the bold pitcher plant, have a more domineering side hidden away. Secrecy, perfectionism or an almost obsessive need to prove a point? Well, sometimes it's worth reflecting on the less flattering habits you might not always recognise in yourself.

Ready to meet your botanical shadow self? Let's dive on in...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

January babies like to believe they're in control, but their biggest weakness may be their need to have things go their way. No wonder, then, that the Venus flytrap is their birth month carnivorous plant.

Like this iconic houseplant, you know when to strike, and once you've made up your mind, you can be remarkably difficult to sway. You may have little patience for people who waste your time or challenge your authority.

Your dark side emerges when determination becomes stubbornness and protecting your boundaries turns into shutting people out. You don't always give second chances, especially when you feel someone has crossed you. Why not buy yourself a Venus flytrap from Amazon, then, and spend some time watching it and reflecting on what it says about you?

February belongs to the fanged pitcher plant, which feels wholly appropriate. If this is you, then your imagination is one of your greatest strengths, but it can also help you become someone others struggle to read.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, you know how to draw people in with something fascinating, unusual or irresistible. You may enjoy being unpredictable, keeping parts of yourself hidden and making others work to understand you. And, at your darkest, you can use charm to get your way, leaving people wondering whether they ever really knew you at all.

March babies notice what other people feel, sometimes before they even say it. That sensitivity can make you compassionate, but it can also give you an advantage you don't always use wisely.

Like the sundew plant, you can appear delicate and harmless while holding on tighter than anyone realises. As such, you may struggle to let go of hurt, replaying conversations and remembering every slight. And, when you're wounded, you might use silence, guilt or emotional distance to make others feel the weight of what they've done.

You have a powerful presence and rarely enjoy being told what to do. Indeed, much like the purple pitcher plant, you can draw attention without trying, but your confidence sometimes hides a tendency to rush headfirst into situations you haven't fully considered.

You may mistake resistance for a challenge and disagreement for disrespect. As such, your darker side appears when your need to win becomes more important than understanding others, because you'd rather take a spectacular risk than admit you might be wrong.

Why not treat yourself to a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Store, then? They're colorful and a cute way to keep pests at bay, not to mention a great way to sit and reflect on the qualities you keep hidden from the world.

If this is your birth month carnivorous plant, you prefer stability... but that doesn't mean you're always as easygoing as you appear.

Like the butterwort, your strategy is subtle: you don't need to chase what you want when you can let it come to you. No wonder, then, that you hide frustration behind politeness, hold grudges long after an argument has ended or quietly keep score when you feel underappreciated.

Your shadow side emerges when patience becomes a way to avoid confrontation and kindness becomes a silent expectation of loyalty in return. Hey, that's not a bad thing; there's a reason this pretty houseplant is so good at killing fungus gnats. Time to bag yourself some butterwort seeds from Amazon, maybe?

A post shared by Lucas Brannen (@lucas_2307_)

Are you a June baby? Say hello to your (very unusual) carnivorous plant!

Always curious about people, you thrive on connection... but you may become restless when the excitement fades. Like the spoon-leaved sundew, then, you attract attention through a delicate and inviting appearance while being far more complicated underneath.

You might tell different people different versions of yourself – not out of malice, but because you want to be understood and liked by everyone. This explains why your darker side appears when the need for validation makes your loyalties unpredictable and your promises easier to break.

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Born in the height of summer, July babies care deeply about the people they let into your world, but their loyalty can have a dangerous edge.

If your birth month carnivorous plant is the cobra lily, you present a striking warning to anything that gets too close, and sometimes may convince yourself that you know what's best for the people you love, even when they haven't asked for your help.

No surprises, then, that your shadow side emerges when protection becomes control, jealousy disguises itself as concern and you struggle to accept that the people you love have the right to make mistakes without your permission. Time to pick yourself up some cobra lily seeds from Seedville, then, and pour some love into it.

A post shared by Mobile Bay National Estuary Program (@mobilebaynep)

August belongs to the white-tipped pitcher plant, which means that you (much like your carnivorous friend here) know how to make an impression, and you rarely enjoy being overlooked. Indeed, much like the white-topped pitcher plant, you have a dramatic presence that naturally draws the eye.

Beneath that confidence, though? Well, you may be more dependent on admiration than you care to admit. You might turn everything into a competition, struggle when someone else takes the spotlight, or dismiss criticism as jealousy. Perhaps, then, your darkest tendency is believing (strike that: knowing!) you're exceptional means you should always get your way.

September's birth month carnivorous plant is the rabbit-eared bladderwort, which is incredibly fitting. After all, you notice everything: the inconsistency in someone's story, the mistake everyone else missed, the detail that doesn't quite add up.

Like the water-dwelling bladderwort, your most interesting mechanisms operate largely out of sight. You may appear helpful while mentally cataloguing other people's flaws but, when things don't meet your standards, frustration can turn into criticism, and careful planning can become an obsession with controlling every possible outcome.

Your shadow side, then, is the belief that if you can find a flaw in everything, nothing can ever catch you off guard. An oddly comforting notion, right?

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Halloween month (this author's birth month, no less!) belongs to the bowl pitcher plant, a particularly fitting match for anyone who happens to be a little, or a lottle, emotionally evasive.

Oh sure, you know how to keep the peace, but sometimes harmony matters to you more than honesty. Like the bowl pitcher plant, you can thrive in ways that others don't immediately understand; think concealing your real feelings, avoiding difficult conversations or telling yourself that keeping your options open is better than making a decision.

Your darker side emerges when diplomacy becomes avoidance and your desire not to upset anyone leaves others guessing where they truly stand with you.

November babies get a twist on a classic carnivorous plant, in the form of an all-red variety of Venus flytrap. Why? Well, because you rarely feel things halfway. When someone earns your trust, you can be fiercely loyal; when they betray it, you may find forgiveness far more difficult.

Like the Red Dragon Venus flytrap, your dark coloring conceals a mechanism that reacts decisively when triggered. You might dwell on betrayal, replay old arguments or become fixated on proving that someone underestimated you, which means your shadow side appears when you stop seeking closure and start wanting the other person to feel the same hurt you experienced. Eek.

A post shared by 8 Billion Trees (@8billiontrees)

Last but not least, December belongs to the corkscrew plant, which means you are something of an escapist as you crave discovery, freedom and the feeling that something exciting is just around the corner.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, whose unusual traps lead prey through a one-way route, your own curiosity can take you further than you intended. You may chase new experiences whenever life becomes predictable, abandon plans when they start to feel restrictive or use humor to dodge uncomfortable truths.

Occasionally, your darker side emerges when freedom becomes an excuse to run from responsibility, as every new beginning becomes a way to avoid finishing what you started.

Whichever birth month carnivorous plant you are, and whatever shadowy trait it holds bare to the light, rest assured that you are still a wonderful person (just check out all of your amazingly positive traits in your classic birth month flower).

Still, there's no denying that it can be fun to embrace our dark sides every once in a while... especially if it helps us embrace a whole new world of plants in the meantime. All hail, then, the bitey side of the botanical world! Sometimes, it's good to be bad...

#8188. Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”

The sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential issues.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8187. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”
